candidates.title: Enabling large language models for automated compliance checking of BIM models in architectural engineering through semantic modelling and linking
candidates.abstract: Purpose This study examines how standardised Building Information Modelling (BIM) data modelling can support large language models (LLMs) in automated compliance checking of architectural project information requirements. The focus is the Level of Information Need (LOIN) for design deliverables. The study addresses the disconnect between LLM reasoning and standardised project information. Design/methodology/approach A constructive research approach is adopted to develop and evaluate an LLM-based compliance checking framework. BIM resources and LOIN-based requirements are transformed into semantic data through information modelling and linking. An Information Container for Linked Document Delivery (ICDD) organises project documents and semantic links. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects LLM interaction with graph querying, compliance checking and issue reporting services. The prototype uses data from a single architectural project. A controlled benchmark compares direct review, Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and MCP review. Findings Direct review based on raw Turtle snippets showed limited performance because compliance evidence was often interpreted conservatively. Graph RAG achieved higher checking performance through structured graph retrieval, while MCP review achieved the best overall result by combining LLM-based task interpretation with tool-mediated checking. Performance varied across rule types. Explicit-data and derived-value rules were checked more reliably than extended data-structure rules, which were sensitive to alternative relation patterns. Originality/value This study presents a prototype approach to BIM–LLM integration for compliance-oriented project information management. Project resources, information requirements and checking rules are organised through ICDD and semantic graph data. MCP-mediated interaction links requirement interpretation with executable checking services, evidence retrieval and issue reporting, enabling traceable compliance review in project delivery.

candidates.title: Neuro-symbolic AI for proactive risk forecasting: bridging large language models and dynamic Bayesian networks
candidates.abstract: Purpose Periodic risk reports constitute a substantial repository of operational data for project management. Despite the inherent informational value, archived records remain largely unstructured and highly fragmented. This study proposes a fully local neuro-symbolic approach for dynamic risk forecasting by translating qualitative project narratives into a quantifiable predictive engine to support decision-making. Design/methodology/approach The proposed methodology adopts a mixed-methods architecture including four layers: (1) spatial morphology reconstruction using a Y-axis density clustering algorithm; (2) a hybrid pseudonymization filter; (3) a local large language model (LLM) with chain-of-thought reasoning; and (4) a symbolic causal engine powered by a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) to quantify causal propagation into a dynamic risk index. Findings An empirical evaluation across 28 reporting cycles spanning a 33-month large-scale infrastructure project indicates that the symbolic layer provides a temporally coherent aggregation of the output of a zero-shot perception layer operating at a macro F1-score of 53.62%. By quantifying causal risk propagation, the DBN captured a 93.59% risk-saturation state, for which the retrieved evidence identifies chronic site-clearance bottlenecks. Notably, using an alert threshold selected by sensitivity analysis together with an analytic constraint on the posterior mass attributable to the critical state (talert = 70.0%), the model outputs Bayesian probabilities alongside LLM-extracted textual evidence, yielding an anticipation interval of 1.33 reporting cycles relative to the documented administrative response. Originality/value The neuro-symbolic framework bridges the gap between deep learning perception and causal inference in construction management. By coupling LLM-driven zero-shot ordinal extraction with DBN causal reasoning, the research establishes an auditable framework for risk documentation. The integrated framework transitions AI from an opaque prediction model into an accountable decision-support tool, providing stakeholders with transparent explainable AI diagnostics and supporting a shift from reactive mitigation to proactive, evidence-based risk prevention.

candidates.title: Large language model responses to postoperative questions in oral and maxillofacial surgery: a comparative evaluation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as patient-facing informational tools in dentistry, but their suitability for postoperative communication in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMFS) remains uncertain. This study compared ChatGPT-5.4 Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Gemini 3 (Thinking mode) in answering routine postoperative OMFS questions. Methods Thirty standardised open-ended postoperative questions were submitted once to each model through public web interfaces using the same neutral prompt. Three OMFS surgeons, masked to model identity, independently rated overall informational quality using an adapted 5-point Global Quality Score (GQS). Factual accuracy, completeness, and clinical safety were rated against a question-specific Reference Answer and Safety Framework; all responses were reassessed after peer review, and both rating sets were analysed. Five readability indices and user-interface latency were recorded. Friedman tests with Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon post hoc tests were used. Results GQS inter-rater reliability was excellent [ICC(2,1), 0.900–0.926]. Mean GQS differed across models ( p < 0.001): Gemini 3 (Thinking mode) 4.82 ± 0.38, DeepSeek-V3.2 4.53 ± 0.49, and ChatGPT-5.4 Thinking 4.08 ± 0.64. Original accuracy and completeness ratings showed limited agreement [ICC(2,1), 0.379 and 0.272]. Factual accuracy differed in the original ratings ( p = 0.014) but not after reassessment ( p = 0.115); completeness did not differ. Of 90 responses, 89 were classified as Safe; one Gemini response on clopidogrel resumption was classified as Missed Red Flag/False Reassurance. After adjustment for word count, Gemini retained higher GQS than both other models (both p < 0.001). Gemini responses were generally more linguistically complex. Observed latency was shortest for DeepSeek-V3.2 (10.49 ± 1.95 s) and longest for Gemini (31.46 ± 11.60 s) and does not represent intrinsic model speed. Conclusions Gemini 3 (Thinking mode) achieved the highest expert-rated informational quality, but between-model differences in factual accuracy were not robust to reassessment, completeness did not differ, and one clinically consequential safety concern was identified. The findings are limited to simulated, single-turn, English-language first responses and do not establish patient comprehension or real-world safety. LLM-generated postoperative information should remain under professional oversight.

candidates.title: Assessing bias in the use of large language models in healthcare: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their growing adoption across domains, including healthcare. However, these models risk amplifying existing healthcare disparities. This systematic review synthesizes the existing literature on bias assessment in LLMs applied within the healthcare domain. We searched six databases, namely, Scopus, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library, for studies published between January 2020 and May 2025, with the final search conducted on 16 May 2025. Retrieved records were screened according to predefined criteria, resulting in 74 included articles. Methodological quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross-Sectional Studies. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were described narratively. LLMs were applied across various healthcare contexts, most notably in medical question answering. Bias assessment methods ranged from human evaluations to statistical analyses, while only 13.5% of the included studies implemented mitigation strategies, which were primarily prompt-based. Overall, 87.8% of the studies reported evidence of bias, with demographic bias being the most commonly investigated bias type. The included studies were of predominantly high quality with minimal risk of bias. The findings indicate that bias remains prevalent in LLM healthcare outputs, highlighting a critical challenge to their equitable and responsible deployment. Future studies should prioritize robust bias evaluation and the implementation of effective bias mitigation strategies to support the safe integration of LLMs into healthcare.

candidates.title: Simulation-Based Basic Life Support Training: A QuasiExperimental Study Comparing Peyton’s Four-Step Approach with Traditional Teaching Among Undergraduate Medical Students
candidates.abstract: Background: Basic Life Support (BLS) competence is an essential requirement for medical graduates; however, traditional teaching may provide limited opportunities for active learning and structured practice. Peyton's FourStep Approach (PFSA) is a learner-centred method for teaching procedural skills, but evidence regarding its effectiveness in BLS skill acquisition and retention among undergraduate medical students in India remains limited. Objectives: To evaluate the effectiveness of Peyton's Four-Step Approach compared with Traditional Teaching Method (TTM) in improving immediate BLS skill performance and one-month skill retention among undergraduate medical students. Secondary objectives were to assess learner satisfaction and confidence with the two teaching methods. Methods: A quasi-experimental study was conducted among 100 third-year undergraduate medical students at GSL Medical College, Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh. Participants were non-randomly allocated into an experimental group receiving BLS training using Peyton's Four-Step Approach (n = 50) and a control group receiving Traditional Teaching Method (n = 50). BLS skills were assessed using a 15-item Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) checklist before training, immediately after training, and one month after the intervention. Student satisfaction and confidence were also assessed. Data were analysed using independent samples t-test and Chi-square test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: Baseline OSCE scores were comparable between the PFSA and TTM groups (5.82 ± 1.34 vs. 5.68 ± 1.41; p = 0.612). The PFSA group demonstrated significantly higher immediate post-training OSCE scores than the TTM group (12.46 ± 1.18 vs. 10.84 ± 1.47; mean difference: 1.62; p < 0.001). At one-month follow-up, skill retention remained significantly higher in the PFSA group (11.72 ± 1.29 vs. 9.63 ± 1.58; mean difference: 2.09; p < 0.001). Student satisfaction was higher in the PFSA group than in the TTM group (90% vs. 16%; χ² = 54.96; p < 0.001). Similarly, a greater proportion of students in the PFSA group reported confidence in performing BLS skills (88% vs. 10%; χ² = 30.43; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Peyton's Four-Step Approach was more effective than Traditional Teaching Method for improving immediate BLS skill performance and one-month skill retention among undergraduate medical students. The approach was also associated with greater student satisfaction and confidence. Incorporating structured, learnercentred approaches such as PFSA into undergraduate BLS training may enhance the acquisition and retention of essential resuscitation skills.

candidates.title: When Similarity is Not Enough: Deterministic Retrieval Pathways for Wellbore-Accurate Knowledge Synthesis on the Volve Field
candidates.abstract: This study compares similarity-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with deterministic retrieval pathways for question answering over the 1,266 public daily drilling reports of Equinor's Volve field. The objective is to establish where embedding similarity is an adequate retrieval mechanism for an identifier-dense operational archive, and where it has to be replaced by the explicit structure the reports already carry, so that an answer about a named wellbore cannot come from a neighboring sidetrack. Reports rendered from the Wellsite Information Transfer Standard Markup Language (WITSML) were parsed into typed sections and organized as a hierarchical corpus tree spanning field, wellbore, report, and section, yielding 7,564 retrievable section chunks. A rule-based router classifies each query and lifts exact filters for wellbore, date, year, section, operator, and rig. Structured intents are answered by walking the tree deterministically, while conceptual intents retain dense and lexical retrieval under weighted rank fusion, and a metadata gate restricts every well-named query to the named wellbore before any ranking. Performance was assessed on 114 queries generated from the corpus across six classes, using recall@10, mean reciprocal rank (MRR), nDCG@10, set precision, recall, F1, date ordering, and a wrong-well rate. Similarity-only configurations proved inadequate for the structured questions that dominate this corpus. The best similarity baseline reached recall@10 = 0.16 on section navigation and F1 = 0.44 on report aggregation, and no similarity configuration returned a chronology in date order, while the deterministic pathways scored 1.00 on all three. On identifier lookups the gated system retrieved the named report at recall 1.00, against 0.18 for the strongest ungated ranker, with a wrong-well rate of zero, and routing lifted within-well operational correlation from F1 = 0.33 to F1 = 0.75. Ungated lexical ranking drew results from the wrong wellbore on 84% of identifier queries and on 52% of structural queries, which confirms that wrong-well retrieval is not confined to neural encoders. A controlled tokenizer comparison placed sibling wellbore identifiers at a mean cosine of 0.32 under subword character n-grams against 0.15 for unrelated identifiers, while identifier-preserving word tokens held both at 0.00, and gating returned the subword encoder to a wrong-well rate of zero. Conceptual paraphrase marks the boundary of the deterministic claim, where the tree alone scored 0.00 and the routed system retained recall@10 = 0.17.

candidates.title: Segment-Level Grounding: Retrieval Triggered by an Uncertainty Signal
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces hallucinations by grounding generation in external evidence, but standard RAG retrieves for every query regardless of necessity. Self-RAG addresses this by training the model to retrieve adaptively through reflection tokens. We propose a complementary approach: segment the generated response, detect uncertainty at the segment level, and retrieve only for the marked segments. Confirmed evidence is injected into the marked segment, after which confidence is recomputed. The approach works with black-box outputs and requires no fine-tuning. This is a position paper: we define segmentation levels, uncertainty-detector features, the injection format, axioms for confidence recomputation, and an evaluation protocol on HaluEval and TruthfulQA with a baseline that isolates the contribution of the trigger.

candidates.title: Query Suggestion for Text-to-Image Retrieval
candidates.abstract: The challenge of translating a user's information need into an effective search query is fundamental in modern cross-modal retrieval systems, which allow users to search image collections with natural language but often lack interactive refinement tools. Our paper addresses the gap by investigating Cross-modal Query Suggestion, the task of dynamically generating targeted query alternatives that verbalize the semantic content of visually coherent image groups within an initial retrieval result set. Building upon our prior work establishing a dedicated benchmark, this extended study systematically compares three distinct methodological paradigms for generating these suggestions: i) latent-conditioned generation, which operates on visual embeddings; ii) caption-based generation, relying on textual abstractions of the result set; and iii) image-conditioned generation, which directly utilizes representative images from the result set as input for Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). We further expand the evaluation framework by introducing new metrics for semantic fidelity against human annotations and computational efficiency. While our evaluation assumes a controlled setup with disjoint image clusters, we validate its robustness against automated partitioning and noise. This work establishes a comprehensive evaluation framework to map the structural trade-offs of these paradigms, and validates the effectiveness of the proposed protocol with a tailored user preference study. Our experiments demonstrate that approaches utilizing direct visual grounding via LMMs produce more image-specific suggestions, Large Language Models (LLMs) reach the best tradeoff between the assessed properties, while latent-conditioned methods have the lowest computational cost. These findings offer critical insights for developing dynamic, visually informed interactive search systems. The dataset, the methods implementations and the code to replicate our experiments are available at: github.com/Ruggero1912/CroQS-benchmark

candidates.title: Generative artificial intelligence drives large model generation algorithm for enhancing Chinese modern traditional cultural knowledge
candidates.abstract: Abstract To address outdated knowledge, cultural-context mismatch, weak evidence linkage, and unsupported expansion in general-purpose large language model generation of traditional-cultural content, this study proposes a generative AI-driven knowledge-enhanced generation algorithm. The method decouples a frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generator from an external dynamic knowledge base and uses a four-field semantic tag scheme covering cultural category, historical stage, regional origin, and application scenario. Candidate evidence is ranked by vector similarity, graph relations, tag consistency, source credibility, and conflict penalties, then assembled into a constrained prompt without modifying the internal attention layers of the frozen model. An incremental update mechanism combines source verification, conflict detection, and expert review, while factual consistency, cultural-context adaptability, and evidence coverage are used for post-generation verification. Experiments cover classical texts, cultural heritage objects, intangible cultural heritage crafts, traditional Chinese opera, and folk culture, with 1,080 factual question-answering samples and 360 contextual generation tasks. The proposed system achieves 88.61% factual accuracy, 95.28% answer relevance, 94.17% evidence faithfulness, and 92.50% cultural-context adaptability. After knowledge updating, accuracy on update-dependent questions rises from 58.67% to 91.33%. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides a traceable, context-sensitive generation pipeline while retaining a frozen generation model; between-system differences are interpreted descriptively because complete paired baseline predictions were not retained.

candidates.title: A Multi-Modal Retrieval Pipeline for Oil & Gas Engineering Workflows
candidates.abstract: Abstract This paper addresses the industry's struggle with legacy technical documentation and labor-intensive manual information retrieval by proposing a multi-modal retrieval framework. The primary objective was to develop a specialized preprocessing pipeline that acknowledges the diverse modalities of O&G documents. By integrating a digital twin logic via the DEXPI standard, our work aims to improve retrieval fidelity, reduce manual lookup overhead, and ensure operational safety within high-stakes engineering environments through deterministic topology injection. We propose a framework utilizing a two-stream methodology to process distinct O&G data taxonomies. The first stream employs a managed cloud OCR service for high-fidelity textual extraction while preserving the structural integrity of documents. The second stream transforms P&IDs into a Multi-Directed Knowledge Graph through a four-phase pipeline: XML sanitization, hybrid attribute extraction, topological mapping, and semantic condensation. This deterministic approach preserves physical connectivity and equipment hierarchies, producing a GraphML-serialized digital twin of the plant topology. An agentic router directs incoming queries to the appropriate stream based on query intent. We conducted a comparative evaluation of three retrieval strategies: a Schema-Driven GraphRAG, Hierarchical GraphRAG, and a Vision Language Model baseline, evaluated across a three-tier query taxonomy spanning attribute retrieval, topological reasoning, and system-level reasoning. Empirical evaluation demonstrated that the Schema-Driven GraphRAG pipeline significantly outperforms both Hierarchical GraphRAG framework and the VLM baseline across all retrieval benchmarks. Achieving an MRR of 0.556 and NDCG@5 of 0.536, with a faithfulness score of 0.99 and answer relevance of 1.00, this approach ensures retrieved context is grounded in verified engineering data. Crucially, while the hierarchical graph model suffered from an 18.3% fatal hallucination rate, caused by probabilistic filling of data gaps in community summaries, the Schema-Driven approach yielded zero hallucinations across 100 queries. Further analysis revealed a 16% reduction in Total Cost of Ownership compared to the hierarchical graph approach, establishing it as both the most accurate and most capital-efficient strategy. This work makes three novel contributions to the field of industrial AI. First, it introduces a unified multi-modal preprocessing framework that bridges unstructured enterprise text and topological engineering drawings within a single retrieval pipeline for O&G environments. Second, it presents an enhanced four-phase DEXPI transformation pipeline that addresses real-world legacy file limitations overlooked by prior work, including vendor-specific XML export quirks and semantic degradation during parsing. Third, it provides a quantitative benchmarking of P&ID retrieval strategies across retrieval accuracy, hallucination density, and total cost of ownership, establishing a validated, capital-efficient blueprint for safe industrial AI deployment.

candidates.title: Retrieval Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation with LangChain: A Comparative Study of Chunking, Sparse, Dense and Hybrid Search
candidates.abstract: This paper compares retrieval strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines built with LangChain. Using the SQuAD v1.1 validation set (48 Wikipedia articles, 1,000 sampled questions), it evaluates three chunk sizes (250, 500 and 1,000 characters, 10% overlap) with three retrievers: BM25 sparse search, dense search using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and hybrid search that fuses both rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Performance is measured with Hit@1, Hit@3, Hit@5 and MRR@10. Hybrid retrieval gave the best Hit@5 (93.1%) and the best MRR@10 at the 250- and 500-character chunk sizes. BM25 was the strongest at Hit@1 and MRR@10 with 1,000-character chunks (77.5% and 0.837). Dense search alone was weakest at every chunk size. The results give practical guidance on chunking and retriever choice for RAG systems.

candidates.title: Multi-dimensional hierarchical temporal alignment for improved temporal commonsense reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

candidates.title: Diagnostic accuracy of multimodal large language models for radiographic interpretation in oral and maxillofacial surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
candidates.abstract: This is a retrospective registration of a completed systematic review and meta-analysis. Searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and quantitative synthesis were carried out between 15 September and 31 October 2026, and the registration records what was done rather than what was planned. A deviations section lists every change made during the review, with the date and the reason for each. The review asks how accurately general-purpose multimodal large language models interpret radiographs in oral and maxillofacial surgery. Web of Science (SCI-EXPANDED), Scopus and PubMed were searched on 30 October 2026; 1,742 deduplicated records were screened and 16 studies, published in 2025 and 2026, were included. Because most reports do not provide a complete 2x2 table, the studies form three overlapping pools: complete 2x2 data, every study reporting sensitivity, and classification accuracy. Classification accuracy is stratified by answer format, since a binary question, a closed multi-class question and an open-ended free-text question do not estimate the same quantity. Accuracy is compared with two benchmarks: uniform guessing and the no-information rate. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 for each of the 19 estimate profiles. The analysis dataset, every script and the full console output are archived with this registration, and one command reproduces every reported numberAuthors: Ahmet Ferhat Büyükdeniz (Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, Faculty of Dentistry, Dicle University, Diyarbakır, Türkiye; ferhat16150101@gmail.com; first author and corresponding author); Mikail Atabay (same department; dt.mikailatby@gmail.com).

candidates.title: HiRAG: A Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework via Intent Routing and Small-Model Refinement
candidates.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates large language model (LLM) hallucinations, traditional flat vector retrieval in massive, heterogeneous databases suffers from high latency and noise interference. To address this, we propose HiRAG, a hierarchical RAG framework. Offline, HiRAG builds a “classification-summary” dual-layer index to structurally organize data. Online, a lightweight bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)-based router identifies query intent to dynamically prune the search space. A cascaded pipeline then uses hybrid retrieval and Small-LLM reranking for coarse-to-fine de-noising. Experiments on the Microsoft Machine Reading Comprehension (MS MARCO) and Multi-Domain Enterprise Knowledge Base (MDE-KB) datasets demonstrate that HiRAG outperforms traditional baselines. Specifically on MDE-KB, HiRAG improves Recall@5 by 14.5 percentage points over Naive RAG and achieves a retrieval augmented generation assessment (RAGAS) Answer Relevance score of 0.92, while reducing average query latency by 28%. HiRAG provides a viable, efficient solution for large-scale knowledge bases.

candidates.title: Authorization-Aware Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Secure Enterprise Knowledge Access
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to answer enterprise questions using external documents; however semantic retrieval and multi-agent delegation create authorization risks when access checks occur only after search or answer generation. This study presents a literature-informed architecture for authorization-aware multi-agent RAG in which a policy decision point evaluates current user and resource attributes, whereas a policy enforcement point restricts the eligible candidate set before content reaches rerankers, agents, or a large language model. This design combines role-based and attribute-based access control, semantic embeddings, vector search, least-privilege delegation, provenance-aware auditing, and policy revalidation at protected access boundaries. A focused survey identifies risks including semantic overfetch, cross-domain synthesis leakage, stale permissions, and delegation escalation. The paper defines authorization-correctness conditions and proposes an evaluation protocol that compares authorization-first retrieval with a retrieve-then-filter baseline. The metrics include unauthorized-context exposure, authorized Recall@k, answer relevance, latency, revocation propagation time, delegation violations, and audit completeness. This study is a survey and design contribution; no benchmark results are claimed because the proposed prototype has not yet been empirically evaluated.

candidates.title: Understanding clinical reasoning variability in medical large language models: a mechanistic interpretability study
candidates.abstract: Medical large language models (LLMs) achieving high benchmark accuracy exhibit unexplained variability in clinical tasks, producing errors that clinicians cannot safeguard against. We evaluated clinical reasoning stability in GPT-5, MedGemma-27B-Text-IT, and OpenBioLLM-Llama3-70B using 355 systematic perturbations of physician-validated oncology cases and trained sparse autoencoders on 1 billion tokens from 50,000 MIMIC-IV clinical notes to decompose their internal representation. We find models exhibit dramatic reasoning instability, shifting staging accuracy by over 50% based solely on prompt format, or generating definitive staging in clinically insufficient scenarios. Sparse autoencoder analysis revealed hierarchical encoding in MedGemma, where high-magnitude features encode lexical identity and low-magnitude features encode contextual meaning. OpenBioLLM distributes information uniformly. We demonstrate these internal encoding structures differentially affect retrieval interventions, suggesting interventions effective for one architecture may harm another. We recommend healthcare institutions implement architecture-specific safety validation, as benchmark equivalence does not imply functional equivalence, with implications for AI safety beyond healthcare.

candidates.title: A Survey on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-PDF Question Answering Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively separates knowledge retrieval from generation for private document question answering. This study explores the design space of document-grounded QA and details a multi-PDF RAG system. The pipeline uses PyMuPDF for text extraction with OCR fallback, BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 for dense embeddings, and ChromaDB for storage. Semantically similar chunks are retrieved via cosine distance to generate answers using a local Llama 3.2:3B model via Ollama. Built with React/Vite and FastAPI, the system supports document management and query APIs. The paper reviews RAG methodologies—including hybrid retrieval, reranking, and GraphRAG—while maintaining a local, modular architecture optimized for consumer-grade hardware. Finally, it evaluates the system's strengths and limitations to identify future research directions.

Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite is selected for its low-latency, cost-efficient characteristics, operating with a 1,048,576-token input limitand 65,536-token output limit. candidates.title: EMASFL: Ensemble of Multi-Agent Small Language Models for Local Fault Localization
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) have significantly advanced Fault Localization (FL) in software debugging but face challenges regarding data privacy, high API costs, and latency. While Small Language Models (SLM) offer a fast, secure, local alternative, they typically lack the reasoning capabilities required for autonomous software repository exploration. This paper proposes EMASFL, a novel local FL system integrating multi-agent architecture with ensemble method. EMASFL overcomes SLM limitations by decomposing the debugging process into a four-step structured workflow executed by specialized agents. The system employs a hybrid strategy, assigning distinct SLM to agents based on their specific strengths in following instructions or code understanding, and integrates outputs from diverse agent configurations using an ensemble method. Evaluations on the Defects4J benchmark demonstrate that EMASFL significantly outperforms existing SLM-based and traditional FL techniques. Notably, it correctly localized 169 bugs, surpassing commercial LLM-based approaches utilizing GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o mini. Operating with an average runtime of 93 seconds and zero API costs, EMASFL provides a practical, high-performance, and privacy-preserving solution for automated software debugging.

candidates.title: Stateful Monitor-Router-Rollback Regulation for Robust Functional Recovery in Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection can divert large language model (LLM) agents from authorized objectives and contaminate subsequent conversational context. We investigate a deterministic Monitor-Router-Rollback (MRR) supervisory controller designed to detect suspicious instructions, constrain execution paths, and reconstruct trusted task context after exposure. The evaluation uses 400 matched attack scenarios, four attack families, three locally served models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 32B, and Mistral-Nemo 12B), seven completed defense conditions, and four recorded phases yielding 33,600 completed model-scenario-defense-phase observations. Our findings demonstrate model-dependent robustness improvements—particularly for Llama 3.1 8B, where automated utility increases from 36.00% to 81.25% under MRR—while establishing rigorous methodological boundaries regarding semantic adjudication, component attribution, and repeated snapshot reconstruction.

candidates.title: A Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architectural Evolution, Key Breakthroughs, and Vertical-Domain Practices
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on massive pretraining based on the Transformer architecture and show significant emergent effects in general tasks. However, the nature of their statically parameterized knowledge causes vertical-domain applications to face three core bottlenecks: knowledge hallucination, delayed timeliness, and loss in long contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) realizes the decoupling of computational logic and factual memory through the paradigm of “retrieve first and generate afterward”. It can dynamically inject domain knowledge without fine-tuning and has become a mainstream technical path for the implementation of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). This study systematically reviews the evolution of RAG technology from 2024 to 2026, from Naive RAG to Advanced RAG, Modular RAG, and graph-enhanced RAG. It analyzes in depth the breakthrough progress of four key technologies, namely hybrid retrieval, multimodal document parsing, generation control, and lightweight deployment. Combined with typical application cases in complex equipment manufacturing, energy and power, public services, and other fields, it explains the engineering value of RAG. Finally, it discusses the evaluation system, existing limitations, and future trends, providing a reference for academic research and practical implementation of RAG technology.

candidates.title: Multimodal Large Language Model-Enabled Healthcare Information System Design
candidates.abstract: Cross-border health-care information systems often struggle to deliver culturally embedded medical knowledge—such as traditional Chinese medicine—to international users with varying health literacy, due to fragmented architecture and weak semantic alignment across languages. This study proposed a tripartite framework built on the Qwen2.5 Vision-Language model at the 7-billion parameter scale, integrating cross-lingual perception, domain knowledge enhancement, and terminology alignment to support multimodal health-care information processing. A bidirectional label-matching feedback mechanism and an entropy-weighted coupling coordination model were developed to quantify system-level synergy. Using 12,642 dissemination records and 7,869 health-care cases (2019–2025), the proposed system outperformed OpenAI's generative pretrained transformer 4o mini by 7.1 points on average across core indicators, with coupling coordination rising from 0.409 to 0.716 and regional synergy gains of 0.382 in Southeast Asia. candidates.title: Large language models in geospatial science
candidates.abstract: Purpose Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context. Findings Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning. Practical implications The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process. Originality/value By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.

candidates.title: Using edge computing and Large Language Models (LLM) for constructing a local agent
candidates.abstract: The growing demand for artificial intelligence systems that are responsive, privacy-preserving, and capable of operating autonomously is driving the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices. However, deploying LLMs as the core of agents on devices with limited resources still faces computational and memory constraints. This research develops an LLM-based local agent architecture that runs locally on a Raspberry Pi without relying on cloud services. The system integrates local LLM inference with agentic functions, including intent processing, reasoning, tool invocation, and interaction with hardware via GPIO. Several quantized Small Language Models (SLMs) were evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16 GB of RAM using CPU-based inference. The evaluation included total latency, Time to First Token (TTFT), token generation rate, peak RAM usage, peak CPU utilization, and peak temperature. The results showed significant performance differences among the models. Qwen 2.5 0.5B Q3 produced the lowest total latency of 23.9 seconds, the lowest TTFT of 269.0 ms, and the highest generation rate of 12.1 tokens/s. However, the results indicate that inference speed alone is not sufficient to determine the most suitable model as the core of a local agent. Most models reached peak CPU utilization above 95%, while RAM usage and thermal characteristics varied across configurations. Based on a combination of inference performance and resource usage, models in the 1B–1.7B range specifically LLaMA 3.2 1B Q4, Qwen 2.5 1.5B Q4, and SmolLM 1.7B Q4 show potential as a balanced set of candidates between responsiveness and model capacity. The research results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying LLMs as local agents on low-cost edge devices and provide a basis for selecting models based on a balance between inference efficiency, resource constraints, and agentic capabilities.

candidates.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
candidates.abstract: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats where attackers trick users through fake emails, websites, or links to steal sensitive information. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, phishing attacks are becoming more realistic and harder to detect using traditional methods. Earlier systems relied on blacklists, rules, and URL features, but recent research explores deep learning, Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal approaches. Explainability and privacy-aware techniques such as federated learning are also gaining importance. The increasing sophistication of phishing campaigns highlights the need for advanced detection frameworks that can analyze diverse information sources simultaneously. Mul-timodal systems leverage text, URLs, visual webpage content, and embedded scripts to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of suspicious activity. Large Language Mod-els further enhance semantic understanding, enabling detection of subtle manipulations in phishing messages. By combining multimodal analysis with explainable and privacy-preserving AI, researchers aim to build adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy solutions that can effectively counter evolving phishing threats in real-world cybersecurity environ-ments.

candidates.title: ASCENT: Scale-complementary external state for frozen long-context language models
candidates.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16 K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is −15.88 points [−20.55, −11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B–8B readers obtain 66.75–85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

candidates.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

candidates.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
candidates.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

candidates.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench

candidates.title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
candidates.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

candidates.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.

candidates.title: Provenance-Aware PCR6 for Conflicting Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must often combine passages that are ambiguous, redundant, or mutually contradictory. This study asks whether proportional conflict redistribution from the Dezert-Smarandache theory (DSmT) provides a measurable advantage over Dempster-Shafer (DS) combination when both rules receive the same evidence and the same control for source dependence. Eight fusion methods were evaluated on 500 RAMDocs (Retrieval with Ambiguity and Misinformation in Documents) questions in three conditions. Under duplicated misinformation, provenance-aware PCR6 (Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule #6) reached 80.6% exact-set accuracy and 92.31% set F1, against 78.2% and 90.98% for provenance-matched DS; the exact-set difference was 2.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [1.2, 3.8]) and the F1 difference was 1.33 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [0.60, 2.33]). With NLI (natural language inference)-derived masses, PCR6 and DS selected identical answer sets, but PCR6 reduced Brier error. A preregistered 1,000-item multi-source experiment using singletons, proper unions, and total ignorance was followed by external validation on 428 RAMDocs items. In controlled partial-ignorance conflict, PCR6+ reduced BetP (betting probability transformation) Brier error from 0.3185 for PCR6 to 0.2733 and remained exactly neutral to an added vacuous BBA (basic belief assignment), although the DS rule achieved the lowest BetP Brier error of the three rules in that same controlled evaluation (0.1878). On the prespecified 260-item RAMDocs applicability subset, ordinary PCR6 had lower BetP Brier error than PCR6+ (0.2354 versus 0.2629), while both achieved set F1 = 0.7718. Exploratory decision sensitivity showed that maximum belief gave PCR6+ its best hard-decision result (exact set 0.5077; set F1 0.7859), whereas DSmP (Dezert-Smarandache probability transformation) sharpened rankings but worsened the RAMDocs Brier score. The evidence therefore supports a bounded claim: PCR6+ corrects a structural multi-source weakness of PCR6 under broad or vacuous focal evidence, but the best fusion and decision rules depend on the downstream loss and the mapping from text to BBAs.

candidates.abstract: This repository contains the complete replication package, empirical datasets, analysis scripts, and high-resolution figures for the research study titled "Quantifying the Fragility of Reasoning in Successive Generations of Large Language Models". Overview & Framework Components Reasoning Predictive Equity (RPE): A metric tracking semantic fidelity via SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2, cosine similarity scaled to [0,1]) against reference trajectories. Fragility Coefficient ($\lambda$): Parameter tracking exponential decay rate over successive generations ($RPE(g) = RPE_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda g}$). Critical Stability Horizon ($g^$): Threshold defined as 50% loss of semantic alignment ($g^ = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda}$). Repository Structure /data/: Empirical CSV datasets, Bayesian HDI fragility records, raw-like checks, and reconstructed parameter tables. /figures/: High-resolution publication-ready figures (300 DPI) including RPE trajectories, stability horizon bar charts, parameter comparisons, and the graphical abstract. /scripts/: Jupyter notebooks and Python scripts reproducing all statistical fits, analyses, and visualizations. /paper/: Compressed draft and manuscript documentation. candidates.title: MLLM-GS: Multimodal Large Language Model Prior-Guided Fast Novel View Synthesis in Extreme Environments
candidates.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. candidates.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. Cascaded passive RLC ladder networks Deterministic Reinforcement Learning Verifier:The package provides an exact, rule-based reward model (laplace_cot_verifier) offering zero-inference-cost reward modeling for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). candidates.title: Code for "The psychophysics of affect in large language models"
candidates.abstract: Code accompanying Marks & Vollberg, The psychophysics of affect in large language models (preprint). This release is the version used for every result reported in the paper. LLMs act as simulated participants: they rate how monetary gains and losses would feel (−50 to +50) and choose between risky gambles and sure options over the same outcomes, in two studies (abstract gambling in GBP; stock trading in % price moves) and three conditions (single-evaluation, memory, joint evaluation). Contents Analysis notebooks: main_study.ipynb (Study 1), study2_stock.ipynb (Study 2) and base_model.ipynb (base model). Each opens with a table mapping its sections to the paper's tables, figures and supplementary material. Precision analysis: power_analysis.py (Supplementary Fig. S1, Table S14). Data corrections: reparse_audit.py and regen_quality.py, which reproduce the re-extraction corrections described in the Methods. Data collection: run_study_batch.py and run_study2_batch.py, with the agents, parsers and quality checks in src/. These run through the OpenRouter API (key required). They are not needed to reproduce the analyses, and the exact responses cannot be regenerated, as some models have since been withdrawn. Result tables: goodness-of-fit and rating-asymmetry tables from the reported runs, in figures/. Reproducing the results Download the data from Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23556542 Place its data/ folder in the repository root. Install the requirements with pip install -r requirements.txt (Python 3.13.5; versions pinned). Run the notebooks from the repository root. Every fit and bootstrap resample is seeded, so results reproduce exactly. The bootstraps take many hours and run in parallel via joblib; the results do not depend on the number of workers. candidates.title: An evaluation of large language models for panoramic radiographs
candidates.abstract: Conversational multimodal models have demonstrated the ability to interpret medical images directly, but their performance on panoramic radiographs has not been systematically evaluated against dental reference standards. We systematically evaluated their ability to identify radiographic findings and localise the affected teeth. Reference labels were established by two experienced dentists, with disagreements resolved by consensus and, when necessary, adjudicated by a senior dentist. We evaluated seven models under zero-shot and four-shot conditions, with three runs per condition. We assessed seven binary tasks and three FDI localisation tasks using macro-averaged accuracy, valid-response rate, conditional F1, and FDI F1, and reported sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value with 95% confidence intervals. The GPT-5.4 family achieved the strongest overall image-level performance, although the leading model varied by task and prompting condition. GPT-5.4-mini achieved the highest four-shot FDI F1. Zero-shot macro-averaged accuracy was highest for GPT-5.4-mini (0.774), and four-shot accuracy was highest for GPT-5.4 (0.778). Compared with zero-shot prompting, four-shot prompting increased macro-averaged accuracy in six of seven models, with a maximum gain of 25.0 percentage points; GPT-5.4-mini decreased by 2.9 percentage points. GLM-4.6V-Flash had the largest increase, accompanied by a 0.383 increase in valid-response rate but a 0.122 decrease in conditional F1. Conditional F1 decreased in six models, and no condition had mean FDI F1 above 0.185. Four-shot prompting improved image-level accuracy in most models, but tooth-level localisation remained poor. This benchmark shows that improved image-level accuracy with four-shot prompting does not ensure reliable tooth-level localisation.

candidates.title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

candidates.title: DolphinRouting: Cluster-Level Binary Routing for Disaggregated LLM Inference Serving
candidates.abstract: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with $k$-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.

candidates.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

candidates.title: Development and Functional Demonstration of MedAnalysis Studio: A Locally Deployed Large Language Model Agent for Medical Research and Statistics Education
candidates.abstract: Objective: To develop a natural-language statistical-analysis agent that integrates a local large language model, specialized medical statistical tools, and output-checking stages, and to illustrate its functionality through representative software-interface displays.Materials and Methods: MedAnalysis Studio version 1.0.1 integrates a locally quantized Qwen2-family model, named EpiMind within the application, with structured tool calls, numerical traceability checks, and methodological auditing. The system provides Chinese and English interaction. Representative single-goal operations are illustrated by preserved screenshots of missingness reporting, correlation visualization, and event categorization.Results: The system comprises 93 configured tools in 12 modules. Illustrative software screenshots show a missingness-report panel, a correlation heatmap, and an event-status display within the natural-language workflow. These examples are presented as interface demonstrations rather than quantitative validation.Conclusions: The integrated workflow connects natural-language requests with explicit statistical operations, checking stages, and structured research outputs. Representative interface displays illustrate the organization of data-quality reporting, visualization, and outcome-category handling. Broader accuracy and clinical performance require separate evaluation.

candidates.title: Comparative evaluation of similarity metrics for Chinese retrieval augmented generation
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance in natural language generation but remain vulnerable to hallucinations, particularly in Chinese short-text tasks where evidence grounding is essential. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a promising solution, yet most prior studies rely on cosine similarity over a single embedding model and focus primarily on English benchmarks. In this study, we systematically evaluate eight similarity metrics—Jaccard, Weighted Jaccard, Dice, character n-gram Jaccard, Sentence-BERT cosine, Euclidean, Manhattan, and Levenshtein—together with two strong Chinese text embeddings (bge-base-zh-v1.5 and m3e-base) within a unified Chinese RAG pipeline. Using the complete CMRC2018 development set (3,219 questions), a second Chinese dataset (DuReader-robust, 1,417 questions), and two deterministically decoded generators (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), we report paired significance tests (McNemar exact; paired bootstrap) with Holm–Bonferroni correction and effect sizes. Four findings emerge. First, strong Chinese embeddings dominate retrieval on both datasets (bge: Recall@4 = 95.3% on CMRC2018, 98.3% on DuReader-robust), showing that the weak retrieval of the multilingual MiniLM SBERT encoder (62.5% on CMRC2018, 68.5% on DuReader-robust) is a property of that encoder rather than of embeddings per se. Second, once a length-bias implementation artifact is corrected, windowed character-level edit similarity attains Recall@4 = 93.8% and end-task F1/EM/grounding statistically indistinguishable from bge—without any embedding infrastructure. This advantage, however, is dataset-conditional: on DuReader-robust’s short keyword-style queries (mean 9.4 characters), which share few verbatim anchors with their source passages, the same lexical metrics fall to 55.8–67.6% and no longer beat even the multilingual SBERT baseline—bounding the scope of this finding to anchor-rich extractive QA. Third, resampling from full-set results shows that evaluations with n ≤ 100 select the wrong best method in up to 37.6% of draws, quantifying the risk of small-sample RAG studies. Fourth, method rankings are stable across the two generators at the tier level (Spearman ρ = 0.70–0.90) while absolute scores are strongly generator-dependent, and a single-threaded computational profile shows that competitive lexical retrieval needs no model weights at 17–22 ms per query, versus a 409 MB encoder and an 8–11 ms per-query encoding pass for the best embedding. For the datasets, encoders, and generators tested, these results provide statistically grounded, hardware-realistic guidance for building efficient and reliable Chinese RAG systems.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Product Design: A Review
candidates.abstract: Product design is a complex, knowledge-based process that balances customer needs with engineering constraints and market realities. While traditional methods such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and machine learning (ML) have improved the design process and solutions, they still struggle with flexibility and a deep semantic understanding of design requirements. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), create new opportunities for intelligent, human-centred support for product design. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review analyzes 1,263 studies published between 2023 and 2026 to answer three questions: (1) how LLMs are applied across design stages, (2) how these systems are evaluated, and (3) what gaps remain. We found that LLMs successfully support design requirements analysis, ideation, and documentation. However, current evaluation methods lack standardized benchmarks for design quality. Persistent challenges remain, including hallucinations, weak domain grounding, tool-integration hurdles, and ethical concerns. To guide future research, we introduce a technical maturity map that highlights current achievements and uninvestigated areas in design systems and suggests a roadmap for applying LLMs in product design.

candidates.title: Correct-option surface profiles and composition sensitivity in industrial multimodal large language model evaluation
candidates.abstract: Industrial multimodal large language model (MLLM) benchmarks summarize performance with one accuracy, although that value also depends on test-set composition. We define a correct-option surface profile from relative word-like segment count, character length, question-option lexical overlap, and special expressions. Using 216,000 frozen responses to 2,400 MMAD-derived items, we audit specification robustness, adjusted associations, and profile-indexed consequences. Adjusted High-Low risk differences are 5.20-5.90 percentage points, but only 19 of 90 model-condition-context cells follow a strict Low-Medium-High order. Empirical composition profiles change standardized accuracy by -0.46 to +0.48 points relative to exact Balanced and produce four local point-order swaps in ten leaderboards, while Top-3 membership remains stable. The surface profile is therefore most informative for composition-aware interpretation of near-tied models, rather than as a stable shortcut-strength scale.

candidates.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
candidates.abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace.ai is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace.ai outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.ai.
