candidates.title: Time-Decay-Aware Reasoning: Maintaining Large Language Model Knowledge Freshness Without Full Retraining
candidates.abstract: Large language models store factual knowledge in their parameters, but this knowledge is fixed at the training cut-off point and becomes outdated as the world changes; therefore, although fluent, the answers may be incorrect. A time-decay-aware reasoning framework has been introduced in this paper to maintain such knowledge over time without retraining or modifying the model’s parameters. The framework assigns a decay rate to each fact based on how often it is updated in a temporal knowledge base, converts this rate into the probability that a parametric answer has expired, and only issues a retrieval call when this probability exceeds a threshold; thus, retrieval is focused on facts that have actually aged. On TempLAMA (50,310 temporally scoped Wikidata questions, 2010–2020), the method outperforms the fine-tuning and editing baselines, recovers about two-thirds of the accuracy gap between a frozen model and exhaustive retrieval while issuing only half as many retrieval calls; it does not modify static knowledge. The Design aims to run large language models efficiently in the face of continuous fact updates.

candidates.title: Text-to-SQL in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey of Reasoning-Centric and Efficiency-Centric Approaches
candidates.abstract: Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into executable SQL, enabling non-expert access to relational databases. Despite advances in large language models (LLMs), reliable systems must ground questions in schemas and values, handle large schemas, and preserve semantic correctness. This survey reviews the evolution toward LLM-based and agentic systems through an objective-oriented taxonomy of Reasoning-Centric (RC) and Efficiency-Centric (EC) approaches. RC emphasizes interpretation, grounding, workflow organization, candidate search, and verification; EC emphasizes acquiring, adapting, transferring, and deploying capabilities under identifiable resource or deployment constraints. Assignments reflect a study’s stated objectives and main contribution, not model size, openness, or training strategy alone. We connect three recurring challenges to ten methodological families and provide an evidence-linked inventory of 114 studies with eleven boundary interpretations. Benchmark-aware comparisons retain model, split, metric, and inference-budget distinctions, including twelve illustrative BIRD development configurations from ten studies. Explicit token values are reported by 31 of 114 studies; a further 6 additional approximate, range, or bound disclosures bring the total to 37, including 16 of the 50 representative studies. Heterogeneous scopes, spanning prompt context, pipeline components, dataset totals, and offline generation, limit direct comparison of end-to-end inference consumption. These findings motivate configuration-specific resource reporting. We also discuss security and safety risks and their evaluation implications. The taxonomy, comparisons, and reporting framework support joint analysis of reasoning quality and resource use in systems combining RC and EC mechanisms.

candidates.title: Systematic Framework of Application Methods for Large Language Models in Language Sciences
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming language sciences. However, their widespread deployment currently suffers from methodological fragmentation and a lack of systematic soundness. This study proposes two comprehensive methodological frame works designed to guide the strategic and responsible application of LLMs inlanguage sciences. The first method-selection framework defines and systematizes three distinct, complementary approaches, each linked toa specific research goal: (1) prompt-based interaction with general-usemodels for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation; (2) fine tuning of open-source models for confirmatory, theory-driven investigation and high-quality data generation; and (3) extraction of contextualized embeddings for further quantitative analysis and probing of model internal mechanisms. We detail the technical implementationand inherent trade-offs of each method, supported by empirical casestudies. Based on the method-selection framework, the second systematic framework proposed provides constructed configurations that guide the practical implementation of multi-stage research pipelines based on these approaches. We then conducted a series of empirical experiments to validate our proposed framework, employing retrospective analysis, prospective application, and an expert evaluation survey. By enforcing the strategic alignment of research questions with the appropriate LLM methodology, the frameworks enable a critical paradigm shift in language science research. We believe that this systemis fundamental for ensuring reproducibility, facilitating the criticalevaluation of LLM mechanisms, and providing the structure necessaryto move traditional linguistics from ad-hoc utility to verifiable, robust science.

candidates.title: Large Language Models (LLMs) for Research Knowledge Discovery
candidates.abstract: The growth of the scholarly literature has posed numerous challenges to knowledge discovery and synthesis and research efficiency. Large Language Models (LLMs), founded on the transformer architecture and other state-of-the-art tools like BERT and GPT-type models, have a tremendous potential to revolutionize the way researchers conduct their scholarly work. This chapter evaluates the role that LLMs play in shaping research practices through literature search, evidence screening, knowledge synthesis, hypothesis generation, and academic writing. The chapter offers an evidence-based review of LLMs in the different stages of the research process with the use of the summary tables on model development, application areas, challenges, and examples from various disciplines. Additionally, critical limitations of the current tools will be discussed alongside suggestions for future directions.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Multimodal Federated Sensing for Compliance Risk Screening in Cross-Border Trade
candidates.abstract: With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. First, an available-modality and quality-adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically weights RGB images, near-infrared (NIR) spectra, and environmental time-series while enforcing strict zero weighting on unavailable modalities and continuous suppression of degraded observations. Second, a regulation-independent state-prototype collaboration and personalized federated learning strategy is developed on a unified continuous concentration scale, enabling cross-institutional transfer of physical contamination representations while avoiding the use of jurisdiction-dependent compliance labels to define shared prototype groups and preserving client-specific adapters against non-IID drift. Third, offline large language model (LLM) parsing transforms unstructured multi-jurisdictional trade regulations into machine-executable rule bases, which are coupled with an uncertainty-aware risk calibration module to dynamically determine exceedance probabilities and reinspection recommendations without retraining front-end sensing encoders when regulatory standards shift. Experimental evaluations on a multisource maize and aflatoxin B1 screening dataset in a workstation-based federated simulation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.054±0.002 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.078±0.003, while elevating the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score to 0.862±0.008 and 0.833±0.009, respectively, reducing the false negative rate (FNR) to 0.121±0.007 (p<0.001). Under severe client heterogeneity and missing-modality scenarios, the proposed approach maintains an AUC of 0.823±0.010 and an F1-score of 0.796±0.011. Ablation and ownership-level analyses assess robustness, calibration (expected calibration error of 0.032), and regulatory adaptation with fixed sensing encoders, providing an end-to-end, traceable decision-support paradigm for international agricultural trade screening.

candidates.title: Jailbreak Connectivity: Towards Diverse, Transferable, and Universal Multimodal Large Language Model Jailbreak
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are vulnerable to visual jailbreak attacks that bypass safety safeguards. Existing methods typically optimize isolated adversarial examples, limiting attack diversity, transferability, and generalization. We propose Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework based on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space. JC optimizes continuous adversarial paths: path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries. On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively. These findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.

candidates.title: Human-in-the-loop annotation and review platform for dental panoramic radiographs: a comparative evaluation of multimodal large language models in tooth-level abnormality detection
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly explored for medical image interpretation, yet their capability for tooth-level abnormality detection on dental panoramic radiographs (OPG) remains largely unquantified. Moreover, reference-standard construction for such evaluations usually lacks a transparent human-in-the-loop review pipeline. We developed an interactive web-based review platform with multi-view visualization (original and annotated images), finding-by-finding auditing, and FDI tooth-number recommendation with accept/reject/manual confirmation, from which an expert-reviewed OPG reference standard of 233 cases, admitted by consensus verification of two senior oral clinicians (1,859 tooth–finding pairs across 1,600 annotated tooth positions; FDI tooth numbers and a closed 20-class disease vocabulary), was derived. On this reference standard, we compared four MLLMs — doubao_web, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, Gemini-3.6-flash-medium and M365 Copilot (GPT 5.6) — on two tasks: tooth-level finding presence and tooth–finding association (classification). The four models were accessed through two arms, an API arm and a consumer web arm, which were not run under matched conditions; within-arm contrasts are the primary inference and cross-arm contrasts are descriptive. Precision, recall and F1 were computed with case-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; paired binary outcomes were tested with exact McNemar tests, re-estimated under case-level cluster-robust variance with Holm correction; per-case F1 with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; and inter-model error independence with Cohen’s kappa. The 233-case evaluation set was drawn from a corpus compiled from an openly licensed public collection together with radiographs acquired at the Department of Stomatology, Yijishan Hospital of Wannan Medical College, with all patient-identifiable information removed before analysis; the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. M365 Copilot GPT 5.6 showed the highest point estimates on both tasks (tooth F1 = 0.642, pair F1 = 0.485), followed by Gemini-3.6-flash-medium (0.610/0.456). Within the web arm, M365 significantly outperformed doubao_web (0.501/0.348; both \(p < 0.001\) ); within the API arm, Gemini significantly outperformed Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (0.537/0.340; both \(p < 0.001\) ). The cross-arm gap between M365 and Gemini was borderline in per-case tooth F1 ( p = 0.052) and remained significant in the tooth-level McNemar test under case-level cluster-robust variance ( p = 0.005; Holm-adjusted p = 0.010). The two strongest models were positively correlated ( \(\kappa\) = 0.316), while all other pairwise model \(\kappa\) values were negative ( \(-0.203\) to \(-0.007\) ), indicating largely independent error patterns. All models performed poorly on caries and periapical lesions (pair F1 < 0.1). Current MLLMs performed relatively better on high-contrast structures (e.g., impacted teeth, F1 = 0.831 for M365, 0.814 for Gemini-3.6) but remained inadequate for subtle lesions; the errors of the four models were largely independent rather than complementary, and a two-model cross-check improved tooth-level union recall from 0.668 to 0.727–0.854 at the cost of arbitrating 20.4–42.3% of positive teeth (a descriptive cross-model quantification, given the unmatched access arms), which supports a two-model cross-check plus human review workflow when that arbitration cost is acceptable. The proposed review platform provides a reproducible, audit-trail reference-standard construction pipeline for benchmarking MLLMs in dental imaging.

candidates.title: Grid-Coded Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Hybrid Retrieval for Minute-Level Aircraft Trajectory Prediction
candidates.abstract: Ultra-short-term (1–5 min) tactical trajectory prediction underpins air traffic conflict detection, yet deep learning models such as long short-term memory (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU) and multilayer perceptron (MLP) networks lack an aviation spatial inductive bias, fit sparse grid-transition samples poorly, and in the small-sample setting studied here incur position errors an order of magnitude larger than trivial baselines. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a natural remedy, replacing parametric fitting with non-parametric retrieval of historical flight priors and requiring no retraining. Existing RAG schemes nevertheless break down on gridded airspace: character-hash encoding of grid identifiers discards spatial semantics, so adjacent grids are treated as unrelated, and the transition prior of the current grid is often missed, while stochastic vector search offers no recall guarantee, so such a miss silently collapses the prediction to persistence. This paper therefore proposes RAG-Hybrid, a grid-coded dual-path framework in which a deterministic breadth-first search (BFS) lookup reconstructs the local transition subgraph of the current grid from the knowledge base, spatially aware FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) retrieval draws on a training-free focal-weighted Gaussian grid vectorisation, and Laplace smoothing with global-Markov weighting calibrates the resulting transition matrix. The evaluation uses Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) trajectories from 62 test flights over a 0.25° × 0.25° grid covering Central–South China, and reports 1 min to 5 min horizons. On this test set, the framework holds single-step Top-1 at 0.7097, identical to a leakage-free global-Markov baseline and within one standard error of the trivial persistence predictor (0.7581), while raising Top-3 and Top-5 at the +1 min horizon from 0.9355 to 0.9839. A constant-velocity dead-reckoning baseline attains the highest point accuracy at this horizon (Top-1 0.8065, MAE 4.90 km) but returns a single cell, so the framework exceeds it on Top-5 by 0.1774. The one component effect that this study resolves statistically is the deterministic lookup channel at the far end of the horizon: removing it cuts the pooled five-step Top-5 hit rate from 0.7452 to 0.6516 and the +5 min Top-5 hit rate from 0.5645 to 0.3710.

candidates.title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

candidates.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

candidates.title: Can large language models complement tourism surveys?
candidates.abstract: Survey studies are central to tourism research, yet declining response rates challenge data collection. Large language models offer a potential alternative for approximating human responses. This study compares four prompting techniques using ChatGPT-4o. At the mean level, chain-of-thought and role-based prompting showed limited alignment with human data, while bias mitigation yielded slight improvement. N-shot learning achieved the strongest mean-level alignment, although performance varied across measures. Analyses of variance, skewness, and kurtosis showed that no prompting technique consistently reproduced human response distributions. These findings identify important boundary conditions: large language models may approximate the “average respondent” on specific measures but fail to capture broader distributional properties, supporting their potential use for early-stage pretesting and screening rather than inference-driven research.

candidates.title: An Automatic Evaluation Model for Health Science Popularization Short Videos Generated by Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Using multimodal large language model (LLMs) to generate and popularize short health-science videos can significantly shorten their production cycle. This practice plays a vital role in lowering the public’s access threshold to health knowledge and promoting the high-quality dissemination of scientific health popularization content. However, due to the limitations of creators, regulators and multimodal LLMs themselves, these generated short videos may still lead to the spread of misleading health knowledge, posing potential risks to public health cognition. Therefore, it is urgent to construct a systematic and automatic evaluation system for such health science popularization short videos. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation model for such short videos by leveraging the well-known Source-Channel-Recipient (SCR) framework in the field of information communication. This automatic evaluation model includes three parts: an automatic review mechanism for Source, an automatic technology-optimization mechanism for Channel, and an automatic feedback-optimization mechanism for Recipient.

candidates.title: A SHAP-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Predictive Maintenance Decision Support
candidates.abstract: Abstract Predictive maintenance models can reach high detection performance, but their outputs often remain difficult to operationalize in industrial environments, where maintenance decisions require interpretability and actionable guidance. Existing approaches rarely establish a direct link between failure predictions, model explanations, and maintenance-oriented recommendations. This study proposes a proof-of-concept framework that extends retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to tabular predictive maintenance data through SHAP-guided query construction. A supervised machine learning model is trained to predict machine failures from operational data. SHAP explanations are then extracted to identify the dominant factors driving each prediction and converted into structured queries. These queries guide retrieval from an experimental maintenance knowledge base using embedding-based similarity search. The retrieved information is used by a generation module to produce case-specific maintenance recommendations aligned with the predictive output and its explanation. The framework is evaluated on a benchmark predictive maintenance dataset, where the predictive model shows strong failure detection capability, with particular improvement in recall for rare failure events. The retrieval module further indicates that explanation-derived queries can retrieve semantically relevant maintenance information. The results support the feasibility of integrating predictive modeling, SHAP-based explanation, retrieval, and LLM-based generation for maintenance-oriented interpretation. The proposed framework remains a proof of concept and does not yet constitute a fully validated industrial decision-support system.

candidates.title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
candidates.abstract: Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

candidates.title: Machine psychology for language models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a "machine psychology" for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

candidates.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
candidates.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Reliable AI Question Answering
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for reliable AI question answering. Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes generate incorrect, unsupported, or outdated information. RAG addresses these limitations by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and using it to generate context-aware answers. This paper explains the fundamental architecture and working principles of RAG, including document preprocessing, embedding generation, vector-based retrieval, context construction, and answer generation. It also discusses the proposed RAG framework and evaluation metrics such as answer accuracy, faithfulness, context precision, context recall, and response latency. Furthermore, the paper examines practical applications of RAG in education, healthcare information, customer support, enterprise knowledge management, and research assistance. It discusses key challenges, including retrieval errors, hallucinations, data quality, security, and computational cost. Finally, it highlights future research directions for improving retrieval quality, evidence grounding, and reliable AI question answering. The paper concludes that RAG can support more context-aware and evidence-based answers, but its reliability depends on source quality, retrieval effectiveness, context selection, and answer verification.

candidates.title: Lookahead Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Predictive Token Selection, Reasoning Control, Knowledge Acquisition, and Long-Horizon Language-Model Decision-Making
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for complex tasks involving multi-step reasoning, long-context understanding, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, software development, autonomous agents, and collaborative problem-solving. Although these systems can generate candidate continuations and evaluate intermediate outputs, a decision that appears locally appropriate may lead to poor downstream reasoning, unnecessary computation, factual errors, tool failures, or incomplete task execution. This paper proposes Lookahead Large Language Models (L²M), a unified research framework for predicting the downstream consequences of candidate language-model actions before committing to them. The framework treats token generation, reasoning-step selection, context management, evidence acquisition, tool invocation, memory operations, model routing, and task termination as decision problems. Given a current state and a set of feasible actions, a lookahead controller estimates their future utility, uncertainty, risk, and computational cost, then selects an action according to an explicit decision objective. The framework separates state representation, candidate generation, outcome prediction, decision selection, execution, verification, and experimental recordkeeping. It can be implemented around an existing language model, incorporated into an inference-time controller, or adapted to training and agent orchestration. A modular Research Slot Architecture is introduced to support independent implementation and evaluation. To facilitate systematic research development, this paper presents 300 candidate research directions across fifteen LLM-specific research categories, including token-level generation, reasoning, context processing, retrieval, tool use, memory, multi-agent systems, code intelligence, mathematics, factual reliability, multilingual behavior, personalization, inference efficiency, evaluation, and model training. The catalogue is intended as a structured research roadmap rather than a claim that every direction is novel or effective. The central hypothesis is that explicit prediction of downstream consequences can improve LLM decisions when candidate actions have materially different future effects and the expected benefit justifies the cost of prediction. This hypothesis requires controlled comparisons against fixed, greedy, heuristic, and learned non-lookahead baselines.

candidates.title: AURORA-RAG: A Trustworthy Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture for Grounded Synthetic Personas
candidates.abstract: Large language models can generate detailed synthetic personas, but unconstrained generation can produce unsupported or contextually inconsistent outputs. We introduce AURORA-RAG, a hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework that incorporates documentary evidence at country–topic, community, community–topic, and persona stages. The system combines dense retrieval and BM25 through Reciprocal Rank Fusion, applies Pseudo-Relevance Feedback, preserves source provenance, and restricts final evidence to indexed corpus passages. We evaluate AURORA-RAG using 1,440 personas across four national environments and three geopolitical topics. Full hierarchical retrieval produces greater downstream conditioning than persona-only retrieval, with mean displacement from no-RAG increasing from .103 to .210. Corpus-supported claims increase from 68% under no-RAG to 82% under single-stage RAG and 91% under full AURORA-RAG, while hallucination frequency decreases from 24% to 13% and 7%. Evidence faithfulness rises from 79% to 90%, attribution accuracy from 82% to 92%, and citation correctness from 85% to 94%. Hybrid RRF achieves the highest observed value on five of six retrieval metrics. These results support hierarchical retrieval as a trustworthy RAG design for improving documentary grounding, reducing unsupported generation, and increasing the auditability of LLM-based synthetic systems.

candidates.title: Adaptive Post-Training Quantization for Language-Centric Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: The growing scale and complexity of language-centric foundation models spanning text, vision, and speech impose substantial storage, memory, and inference costs, motivating post-training quantization (PTQ) for efficient deployment. However, architectural and modality-specific differences govern how quantization affects internal representations and downstream performance, motivating complementary quantization approaches for distinct model structures and sensitivity profiles. This thesis develops separate quantization strategies for weight-centric and joint weight–activation-sensitive architectures. Saliency-Aware Graph-guided Efficient Post-Training Quantization (SAGE-PTQ) targets models where weight compression is the primary objective. SAGE-PTQ preserves salient weights at higher precision while binarizing graph-guided groups of unsalient weights, enabling near-binary representations with low auxiliary overhead. In contrast, Quantization via Adaptive Migration (QAM) targets speech-to-text architectures that are particularly sensitive to both weight and activation characteristics. QAM jointly leverages weight and activation statistics to identify sensitive input channels and adaptively redistribute quantization resolution while maintaining uniform low-bit weights. Across large language, vision-language, and speech-to-text models, the proposed methods preserve task performance while substantially reducing model storage and device-memory requirements. These results demonstrate the importance of adapting quantization strategies to the architectural characteristics and modality-specific sensitivity profiles of language-centric multimodal models.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Systematic Survey of Architectures, Chunking Strategies, and Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Large language models generate fluent text, but they are bounded by the knowledge frozen in their parameters at training time, they hallucinate facts, and they cannot inspect private or fast-changing information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limits by coupling a language model with an external retrieval system: relevant documents are fetched at inference time and supplied as context, grounding generation in verifiable evidence. This paper presents a systematic survey of the RAG literature. It organizes the field into a unified pipeline of indexing, retrieval, augmentation, and generation; compares dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval architectures; examines chunking strategies and their effect on retrieval quality; reviews evaluation methodology, including benchmark datasets, retrieval metrics, and generation metrics; and discusses open challenges such as retrieval failure modes, context-length trade-offs, evaluation contamination, and the economics of maintaining a retrieval corpus. The survey concludes that RAG has shifted the central design problem of language-model systems from model scale alone toward corpus quality, retrieval precision, and evidence-aware generation.

candidates.title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

candidates.title: Tessera: Structure-Completed Evidence Units for Web Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Web retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) splits a page into fixed-size text chunks or, in recent visual pipelines, screenshot tiles, and the retrieved item serves at once as the unit of indexing, ranking, and reading. We trace answer evidence from source HTML to reader input over the full English Wikipedia and find that this coupling loses evidence in text and screenshot pipelines alike: evidence present in the source page often fails to reach the reader intact, particularly structured content such as tables and infoboxes, which chunking separates from the headers and context that give it meaning. Stronger extraction, context expansion, and larger reader budgets leave the loss in place. We present Tessera, a training-free evidence delivery layer that decouples what a pipeline retrieves from what its reader reads. Given the pages behind any ranked list, Tessera rebuilds their HTML into fine-grained evidence units, each completed with its page title, section path, and table headers, selects the units relevant to the query, and packs them into the reader context at an unchanged token budget. The index, the retriever, and the reader stay as they are, so Tessera applies to text, screenshot, and agentic pipelines. Across three question answering benchmarks, Tessera improves answer accuracy by 5 to 6 points on text and screenshot pipelines, consistently across readers, retrievers, and reader budgets, and outperforms strong HTML-aware and structure-aware RAG baselines under matched budgets. The gains carry over to multi-step agentic search. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/sarendis56/Tessera.

candidates.title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
candidates.abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.

candidates.title: Detailed Balance in Large-Language-Model-Driven Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agents are emerging as a powerful new paradigm for solving complex problems. Despite the empirical success of these practices, a theoretical framework to understand and unify their macroscopic dynamics remains lacking. This paper proposes a method based on the least action principle to estimate the underlying generative directionality of LLMs embedded within agents. By experimentally measuring the transition probabilities between LLM-generated states, we report evidence consistent with a tendency toward detailed balance in LLM-generated transitions, indicating that LLM generation may not be achieved by generally learning rule sets and strategies, but rather by implicitly learning a class of underlying potential functions that may transcend different LLM architectures and prompt templates. To our knowledge, this provides an effective macroscopic description of LLM generative dynamics that does not depend on specific model details. This work is an attempt to establish a macroscopic dynamics theory of complex AI systems, aiming to elevate the study of AI agents from a collection of engineering practices to a science built on effective measurements that are predictable and quantifiable.

candidates.abstract: 이미지 내에서 가려진 객체를 완전한 형태로 복원하는 기존 방법들은 고정된 객체 클래스 목록이나 사전 학습된 인식 모델에 의존하기 때문에, 학습 데이터 범위를 벗어난 객체에 대해 탐지 실패가 발생할 수 있다. 또한 이미지 경계를 벗어난 객체에 대해 고정된 비율로만 확장을 수행하여 객체 크기와 위치에 따른 적응적 복원이 어렵고, 마스크 품질과 단순 객체명 기반 인페인팅 프롬프트 역시 복원 성능을 제한한다. 본 연구는 이러한 한계를 완화하기 위해 시각-언어 모델(VLM)을 활용한 가려진 객체 복원 방법을 제안한다. 제안 방법은 이미지 내 객체 리스트를 동적으로 추출하고, 경계 이탈 여부와 확장 방향을 반복적으로 판단하며, 객체 외형 정보를 포함한 프롬프트를 이용해 인페인팅을 수행한다. 더불어 픽셀 유사도 중심의 기존 평가 한계를 보완하기 위해 VLM 기반 객체 완성도 평가 지표를 도입하였다. 실험 결과, 제안 방법은 기존 방법보다 객체 탐지 실패를 줄이고 완전한 객체 형태 복원 성능을 향상시켰다.

candidates.title: Request-Adaptive Execution for Efficient Hybrid LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Hybrid large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising way to combine the modeling capability of the Attention mechanism with the efficiency of state space models (SSMs). However, most existing hybrid LLMs still inherit a static design philosophy: once the Attention-to-SSM layout is chosen, every request must follow the same hybrid execution. This one-layout-fits-all design is inefficient for real-world serving workloads, where different requests rely on contextual information in different ways. This paper presents Morph, a serving system that co-designs the model architecture and runtime for request-adaptive hybrid LLM inference. Its model architecture pairs Attention and SSM layers within each block and uses prefill-oriented gating to select a request-specific layout that remains fixed throughout decoding. Its serving runtime preserves batching efficiency under divergent layer choices through selective batching and enables correct prefix reuse through hybrid-aware context caching. Experiments on six datasets show that Morph achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than existing static hybrid baselines. System-level evaluation further shows that Morph improves the serving throughput by up to 3.87x over baselines while substantially reducing inference latency.

candidates.title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

candidates.title: UniGFM-RAG: Unify Graph Foundation Models and Large Language Models for End-to-End Retrieval and Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across tasks, but they still struggle with complex reasoning that requires integrating scattered knowledge. Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses this challenge by organizing fragment knowledge as graphs, while recent Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) further improve GraphRAG with graph-native retrieval and reasoning capabilities. However, existing GraphRAG methods usually adopt decoupled retrieve-then-generate pipelines, which create objective misalignment between retrieval and reasoning, and training GFM retrievers typically depends on expensive human annotations. To address these limitations, we propose \ourmethod, a unified end-to-end GraphRAG framework that tightly couples a GFM retriever with an LLM generator. Given a query, the GFM retriever first reasons over the graph to score and retrieve relevant document nodes. These node embeddings are then passed through a fully differentiable graph bridge, which projects them into soft-weighted graph prefixes according to retrieval scores and combines them with raw document texts to form graph-augmented prompts. In this way, structural information is injected directly into LLM generation, while the final answer loss can be back-propagated through the bridge to jointly optimize retrieval and reasoning. To stabilize training and reduce reliance on costly annotations, we further introduce a semantic-guided distillation module that provides auxiliary supervision using pseudo-labels derived from query-document semantic similarities. Extensive experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and three out-of-domain GraphRAG benchmarks show that \ourmethod consistently outperforms strong baseline methods and generalizes well, which demonstrates the effectiveness of end-to-end GraphRAG with tightly integrated GFM retrieval and LLM reasoning.

candidates.title: Learning to Remember: Advances in Memory Mechanisms for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

candidates.title: Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.

candidates.title: OneEEG: A Unified Signal-Visual Multimodal Language Model with Task-Aware Mixture of Projectors for Multi-Task EEG Understanding
candidates.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in clinical assessment, brain-computer interfaces, and cognitive-state analysis, yet EEG modeling remains fragmented across task paradigms. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a promising interface for flexible multimodal reasoning, but their ability to understand EEG inputs remains limited. In this work, we propose OneEEG, a unified EEG-MLLM framework for multi-task EEG understanding. By training on our curated OneEEG-Instruct, a multi-task EEG instruction-tuning dataset, OneEEG jointly models numerical EEG representations and visual EEG representations, and introduces a task-aware Mixture of Projectors (MoP) to align heterogeneous EEG features across different task families with the LLM embedding space. We further establish OneEEG-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating current MLLMs and our method on multi-task EEG understanding. Experiments show that existing MLLMs have limited ability to interpret EEG inputs, while OneEEG achieves stronger performance by integrating numerical and visual EEG representations with task-aware EEG-to-LLM projection. Extensive ablations and analyses further reveal the effects of visual EEG renderings, MoP variants, router behavior, and feature dispersion across EEG tasks.

candidates.title: LegalAssist: A Temporally Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Searching Indian Court Judgments
candidates.abstract: Advocates and law students must navigate a large and continuously evolving body of Indian Supreme Court and High Court judgments, yet conventional keyword search and proprietary legal databases create significant limitations in accessibility, semantic retrieval, and reproducibility. General-purpose large language models can provide natural-language legal assistance but remain vulnerable to hallucinated authorities and unsupported claims. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a mechanism for grounding model outputs in an external legal corpus, but retrieval quality alone does not ensure reliable legal answers. This paper presents LegalAssist, an open-source retrieval-augmented generation system for searching Indian court judgments and generating source-grounded legal responses. The system implements a modular retrieval and verification architecture combining query expansion, BM25 lexical retrieval, FAISS dense retrieval using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder reranking, authority-aware ranking, temporal-validity checking, natural-language-inference-based citation verification, and reliability-based answer abstention. Legal answers are generated in a FIRAC (Facts, Issues, Rule, Application, Conclusion) form using GPT-4o-mini or a local Qwen model. The system is evaluated using the Indian Legal Prior Case Retrieval (IL-PCR) task of the IL-TUR benchmark, which provides gold relevance judgments rather than proxy similarity measures. The results show that BM25 remains the strongest retrieval configuration on the evaluated benchmark, with dense retrieval, multi-query expansion, and general-purpose cross-encoder reranking failing to consistently improve retrieval performance. The principal contribution of LegalAssist therefore lies not in replacing lexical retrieval with dense retrieval, but in integrating temporal-validity detection, citation verification, reliability estimation, and abstention into an open and reproducible legal-AI pipeline. The resulting architecture provides a transparent approach to reducing unsupported legal generation while explicitly exposing the limitations of automated retrieval and generation. The study demonstrates how system-level safeguards can be incorporated into legal RAG architectures to improve reliability, reproducibility, and responsible deployment on consumer-level computing infrastructure.

candidates.title: GuardRAG: A Post-Retrieval Defense against Poisoning Attacks in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the factual grounding of Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external evidence, but also exposes them to corpus poisoning attacks. In particular, coordinated attacks can introduce multiple mutually reinforcing poisoned documents into retrieved contexts, making reliable evidence filtering challenging. To address this problem, we propose GuardRAG, a training-free and plug-and-play post-retrieval defense that exploits the semantic structure of retrieved evidence to identify suspicious document groups. Specifically, GuardRAG first expands the retrieval range and removes near-duplicate candidates, then partitions the retained documents using Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC) with a query-adaptive threshold. Finally, it scores and prunes suspicious clusters based on query relevance, cluster size, and semantic compactness. Experiments across three question-answering datasets, multiple poisoning attacks, and six LLMs demonstrate that GuardRAG substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining answer utility under clean retrieval.

candidates.title: Evaluating Evidence Sensitivity and Robustness of Hallucination Detectors in Retrieval- Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the accessibility of external knowledge for large language models, but generated responses can remain unsupported, contradictory, or otherwise hallucinatory. Conventional hallucination-detector evaluation largely emphasizes aggregate benchmark performance, which may not reveal whether detector decisions remain reliable when the evidence distribution changes. This study presents a controlled evaluation of hallucination detectors from an evidence-sensitivity and robustness perspective. Three detector configurations - TF-IDF with Logistic Regression, TF-IDF with Linear Support Vector Machine, and DeBERTa-v3-base were evaluated using RAGTruth, HaluBench, and TRIVIA+. In-domain evaluation on RAGTruth showed that DeBERTa achieved an AUROC of 0.8483 and Macro-F1 of 0.7616. However, performance declined substantially under distribution shift, with AUROC decreasing to 0.5348 on HaluBench and 0.5910 on TRIVIA+. Controlled evidence interventions showed substantial detector responsiveness, with mean Evidence Sensitivity Index values of 0.2641 for evidence removal and 0.3268 for cross-example evidence substitution. A context-complexity stress test further showed progressive degradation as irrelevant evidence increased from 0% to 100% within a fixed 512-token observation window, with AUROC decreasing from 0.8306 to 0.7325 and Expected Calibration Error increasing from 0.1375 to 0.4072. Input ablation demonstrated that both generated answers and retrieved evidence contribute to detection performance. These findings show that benchmark accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize hallucination-detector reliability and motivate evaluation frameworks that jointly assess generalization, evidence sensitivity, contextual robustness, and calibration.

candidates.title: Large language models in personalized oncology
candidates.abstract: Background . Large language models are considered a promising tool for personalized oncology; however, their role in the analysis of molecular data and treatment selection should be clearly distinguished from the functions of specialized predictive models. Objective . To systematize the potential applications of large language models in personalized oncology, primarily for the interpretation of clinical, genomic, and transcriptomic data and of predictions of tumor chemo- and radiosensitivity. Methods . We performed a narrative review of publications identified in PubMed and Google Scholar, with the search updated through July 1, 2026. Original studies and reviews on medical LLM applications, foundation models for genomic and transcriptomic data, clinical decision support, and prediction of anticancer treatment sensitivity were considered. Results . The most justified approach is to use a language model as an interface layer: a specialized machine-learning or deep-learning model calculates the prediction, while the language model generates an explanation, compares the result with clinical guidelines, and indicates limitations. The main risks include unreliable responses, insufficient reproducibility, weak external validation, and legal constraints. Conclusion . A clinically promising architecture separates computation from explanation: the language model does not prescribe treatment autonomously but links molecular data, a validated predictive model, and the physician.

candidates.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation
candidates.abstract: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support. By isolating qualitative LLM reasoning from visual perceptual noise and database metadata sparsity, the system successfully bridges the gap between intuitive meal perception and point-of-care dietary risk triage, offering a non-invasive and scalable solution for automated dietary auditing and longitudinal population health monitoring.

candidates.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Text Summarization
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for abstractive summarization, yet most prior work in evidence synthesis limits summarization to titles and abstracts and primarily focuses on domains with well-structured reporting formats. These limitations restrict the applicability of automated PICO summarization in social science research, where key information is often embedded in unstructured full-text sections. This study presents a comprehensive end-to-end workflow for fine-tuning LLMs for PICO-oriented summarization of long-form scientific texts in the mental health domain. The proposed pipeline integrates document-level annotation, label-specific instance construction, section-aware data augmentation, long-context model architectures, optimization strategies, and multi-metric evaluation within a unified framework. To systematically examine the effects of model and training choices, we employ a 2×3×3 factorial design varying model architecture, batch size, and learning rate. Performance is evaluated using three complementary metrics (ROUGE, perplexity, MAUVE), supplemented by qualitative comparisons between model-generated and human-written summaries. Results show that LongT5 consistently achieves higher ROUGE and lower perplexity, while BioBART attains higher MAUVE. Across configurations, intermediate learning rates and moderate batch sizes yield the most balanced performance. Further analysis reveals that higher learning rates disproportionately benefit structured and quantitative categories, while gains are more limited for descriptive categories. These findings highlight systematic trade-offs between accuracy, confidence, and diversity in generated summaries. Overall, the proposed pipeline provides practical, evidence-based guidance for applying generative models in long-document evidence synthesis and offers a foundation for future research on finetuning LLMs.

candidates.title: Topic-Level Fairness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Group fairness in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems is typically evaluated using metrics aggregated across queries. However, such metrics can conceal topic-level disparities: a system may favor women on questions about human rights and men on questions about actors and filmmakers, appearing nearly neutral overall even though neither topic is fair. We therefore study topic-level fairness, which requires group fairness to hold within each topic rather than only in aggregate. To reduce the topic-level disparity, we adapt the reranker separately for each topic with a Bradley-Terry objective under direct supervision from the generated output: preference pairs built from the generator's own output carry the direction that topic requires. With preference pairs built from RoMQA alone, the adaptation reduces the mean absolute per-topic disparity by 51% on RoMQA and by 40% on TREC Fair Ranking while retaining accuracy. No baseline reaches the reduction, even when modified to treat each topic separately rather than apply one correction to every topic. Neither does our method with one reranker for all topics, which follows the direction that most topics require.

candidates.title: SEVD: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models via Semantic Evidence Verification Decoding
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in visual understanding and open-ended generation, yet they remain prone to hallucination, where generated content is inconsistent with or unsupported by the visual input. Existing training-free decoding methods mainly intervene through token-level generation scores or output distributions, while the semantic content represented by candidate tokens is not explicitly verified. We propose Semantic Evidence Verification Decoding (SEVD), a training-free decoding method that elevates hallucination mitigation from token-level intervention to semantic-level verification. SEVD first constructs explicit semantic units from candidate tokens, performs semantic evidence verification by comparing how the model's support for the same semantic unit changes when visual evidence is preserved, weakened, or removed, and finally maps the resulting outcomes back to decoding decisions through selective intervention. Extensive experiments across different MLLM backbones and benchmarks demonstrate substantial hallucination mitigation while preserving general multimodal capability, supporting the effectiveness and transferability of SEVD. candidates.title: Off‐The‐Shelf Large Language Models Are Unreliable Judges
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT I conduct large‐scale empirical experiments to test the reliability of large language models (LLMs) as legal interpreters. Combining computational methods with the results of a new survey, I find that LLM judgments are highly sensitive to prompt phrasing, output processing methods, and choice of model. I also find that frontier LLMs do not accurately assess linguistic ordinary meaning, and I provide original evidence that tuning base models into assistant models shifts ordinary‐meaning judgments unpredictably and can worsen their alignment with human judgments. These findings undermine LLMs' credibility as legal interpreters and cast doubt on claims that LLMs elucidate ordinary meaning.

candidates.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LaTeX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper and the side at fault; or unfinished, with the reason. The kit follows the paper's own proof step by step, rather than finding a new one. Separate agents write and review, each statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted afterwards, and every verdict rests on evidence that can be rerun without a language model. The kit runs unattended for hours, waits out usage limits, re-checks only what a revision changed and reports its cost by role, model and result. We describe the design, walk through a complete run, and apply the kit to four example papers with answer keys and to three published statistical papers, checked blind in their versions from before public corrections. In all three, the kit found the published error at the step that the correction names, together with further problems that we confirmed by hand. Given the same papers directly, the same language model working with Lean classified fewer results correctly on the longest paper and reported some statements narrower than the paper's as proved; no verdict of the kit claimed more than its Lean evidence showed.

candidates.title: FOCUS: Active Critic Learning for Long-Horizon Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Sparse outcome rewards make it difficult for long-horizon language-model agents to assign credit to earlier actions. Learned critics provide value estimates for intermediate states, but these estimates can be inaccurate, while estimating intermediate values with repetitive continuation samples from points within a trajectory incurs substantial costs. To mitigate these issues, we introduce FOCUS, an RL method that uses selective branching to help the critic network learn its value estimator. The rollout controller facilitates active learning for the critic by sampling continuations from states that are expected to most reduce the critic's estimation error. These refined value estimates then score the segment between consecutive states with a TD($λ$) advantage, while the sampled evidence supplies training targets for the critic. FOCUS supports long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning through a modular context-management interface that decouples context management from rollout allocation. Our experiments show that using compaction-induced segment boundaries for value estimation and credit assignment, FOCUS outperforms GRPO and VinePPO with matched per-step generation budgets on legal reasoning, deep search, and code localization benchmarks, improving held-out accuracy at Qwen3.5-9B scale by 7.2 points over the strongest baseline on BrowseComp-Plus (55.4 vs. 48.2) and by 4.1 points on DeonticBench (56.5 vs. 52.4).

candidates.title: Comparison of large language models in answering early gastric cancer clinical problems and recognizing multimodal endoscopic images
candidates.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in medical information support, but their efficacy in early gastric cancer (EGC) remains under-evaluated. This study systematically assesses LLMs performance in answering EGC clinical questions and analyzing white light endoscopy (WLE) and narrow band imaging (NBI) images. Methods: This study systematically reviewed clinical guidelines and interviewed patients to compile 40 clinical questions and 50 Single-choice questions related to EGC. Ten clinicians and ten EGC patients quantitatively scored LLM-generated responses across four dimensions: accuracy, correlation, completeness, and Comprehension. Readability metrics and Single-choice answer accuracy rates were further calculated. Additionally, the study incorporated 482 white light endoscopy (WLE) and 478 narrow band imaging (NBI) images from four hospitals in China. It systematically evaluated the diagnostic efficacy of different LLMs for multi-task recognition of EGC based on accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC). Findings: In text assessment, ChatGPT-4o achieved the highest scores for accuracy (86), correction (88), and comprehension (88), while Grok-3 scored highest for completeness (90). The accuracy rates for ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini-2.5, and Grok-3 in answering Single-choice questions were 78%, 88%, 76%, and 82%, respectively. candidates.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

candidates.title: An Unsupervised Multimodal Semantic-Enhanced Entity Alignment Method Based on Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal entity alignment identifies equivalent entities referring to the same real-world object across heterogeneous multimodal knowledge graphs and is essential for multi-source knowledge integration. Existing methods often rely on manually labeled seed alignments and multimodal feature similarity, limiting their ability to capture implicit semantic equivalence under heterogeneous attribute and relation expressions. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities for unsupervised alignment, but their direct application remains challenging because of the large entity search space, redundant knowledge graph information, and the stochasticity of LLM inference. To address these challenges, we propose MEA-LLM, an LLM-based fully unsupervised multimodal semantic-enhanced entity alignment method. MEA-LLM first pre-screens candidate entities by jointly exploiting multimodal similarities derived from visual, attribute, and relational information. It then selects discriminative attributes and relations based on degree of freedom, candidate frequency, and discriminability for LLM reasoning. Multiple inference and result aggregation are further employed to improve robustness. Experiments on FB-DB15K and FB-YAGO15K show that MEA-LLM outperforms existing methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Further ablation studies, hyperparameter analyses, experiments with different model-scales, and efficiency evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the core components and indicate that MEA-LLM achieves a favorable trade-off between entity alignment performance and inference cost.

candidates.title: SPARTA: A Sparse Ternary LLM Accelerator with Adaptive Attention and Unified Datapath for Long-Context Edge Inference
candidates.abstract: LLMs on edge devices are constrained by limited memory and bandwidth. Although 1.58-bit ternary weights greatly reduce model storage, long-context inference is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache traffic and attention. Existing accelerators also use separate datapaths for ternary linear layers and attention, incurring hardware and execution overhead. We present SPARTA, a sparse ternary LLM accelerator for efficient long-context edge inference. SPARTA integrates: (1) a phase-aware sparse dataflow exploiting heterogeneous sparsity across compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode; (2) a unified compute fabric mapping ternary SpMM/SpMV and bit-serial attention onto shared processing elements to exploit zero-weight and zero-bit sparsity; and (3) an adaptive two-stage attention engine combining page-level Top-k selection to reduce K-cache accesses with token-level Top-p pruning to reduce V-cache traffic. SPARTA reduces KV traffic by 4.1-4.8x over full attention and 1.3-1.5x over a state-of-the-art sparse-attention scheme, with task-dependent quality loss. Compared with NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, SPARTA achieves 3.9x higher generation throughput and 8.3x higher end-to-end energy efficiency on average; versus AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, the gains are 5.0x and 81.7x. It also delivers 1.6-12.0x higher throughput, 2.0-4.2x higher energy efficiency, and 1.3-51.4x higher area efficiency than FIGLUT, TeLLMe, and MCBP.
