candidates.title: FitCoach: A Multimodal AI-Powered Personal Fitness Coaching System using Human Pose Estimation, Nutrition Intelligence, and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Maintaining a consistent and effective fitness routine requires more than simply following predefined exercise plans, as users often struggle with incorrect exercise form, inadequate personalization, nutritional decision-making, and the lack of continuous feedback. Recent advances in computer vision, deep learning, pose estimation, and artificial intelligence have enabled automated systems for exercise recognition and form assessment. However, many existing fitness applications address these capabilities independently and provide limited integration between exercise monitoring, nutritional analysis, and personalized coaching. This paper presents FitCoach, an AI-assisted fitness coaching system designed to provide an integrated and personalized fitness experience using computer vision and intelligent decision-making. The proposed system utilizes human pose estimation to identify body landmarks and analyze exercise movements, enabling real-time assessment of exercise form and feedback. In addition, the system incorporates food recognition and nutritional information to support dietary monitoring, while user-specific information is considered to generate more personalized fitness recommendations. The system is designed to combine multimodal inputs, including visual exercise information, user activity, and nutritional data, into a unified coaching framework. By integrating exercise-form analysis, dietary awareness, and personalized guidance, FitCoach aims to overcome limitations of isolated fitness technologies and provide users with accessible, adaptive, and intelligent fitness support. The proposed framework demonstrates how computer vision and AI-based personalization can be combined to develop a more comprehensive digital fitness coaching solution.

candidates.title: Explanations, Evidence, and Overreliance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Critical Literature Review
candidates.abstract: The presence of evidence in output generated by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) does not guarantee that the information is correct or that the users will evaluate it properly. This research examines the ethical relationship between explanations, source attribution, and overreliance in artificial intelligence systems. It synthesizes scholarly literature of retrieval and attribution, explanation faithfulness, and human-artificial intelligence interaction. It highlights four properties: factual correctness, evidential support, source credibility, and explanatory faithfulness. The study indicates evidence that explanations can increase acceptance of incorrect answers, however useful sources and lower verification costs can support appropriate reliance. The findings observed in this research do not establish a universal standard of citations or explanations in deployed RAG systems. The review argues that users should maintain the practical ability to question recommendations in responsibly designed systems. A conceptual framework is proposed by connecting evidence presentation to verification effort, opportunities for contestation, and responsibility. Key issues include identifying unsupported claims and source disagreement, distinguishing post-hoc attribution from causal explanation, and evaluating risk controls based on decision outcomes as well as reported trust. The contribution is an interpretation and research agenda, further experiments and empirical research needs to be done to extend this research.

candidates.title: Enabling Efficient Serverless Inference Serving for LLM (Large Language Model) in the Cloud
candidates.abstract: This review report examines the problem of cold-start latency in serverless inference for large language models (LLMs) and surveys recent systems that address it, with a particular focus on ServerlessLLM. In serverless environments, loading multi-hundred-gigabyte LLM checkpoints and initializing GPU resources can dominate end-to-end latency, making real-time applications such as conversational agents and translation services difficult to deploy cost-efficiently. The report first summarizes the cold-start problem and common mitigation strategies in today's Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms, including container warming, host-side checkpoint caching, and cluster-level storage servers. It then reviews the design of ServerlessLLM, which exploits underutilized multi-tier storage in GPU servers, a loading-optimized checkpoint format, live inference migration based on token-level state transfer, and a startup-time-aware model scheduler. Additional methods from recent literature, such as RainbowCake's layered container caching, and the cold-start handling mechanisms of major cloud providers are also discussed. Drawing on the evaluation presented in the original work, the report highlights that multi-tier checkpoint loading and live migration reduce model startup time by up to 6-8× compared to conventional formats, and deliver up to 28× lower startup latency than Ray Serve for large models in realistic traces. The review concludes by outlining open challenges and future directions, including integrating model compression, multi-level inference pipelines, and advanced memory-offloading techniques to further improve the scalability and efficiency of serverless LLM inference.

candidates.title: Do large language models keep the hedge? Uncertainty preservation when large language models summarize aviation and maritime incident reports
candidates.abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

candidates.title: Geometric Parrots: Rule Absence vs. Rule Fragility in Spatial and Physical Reasoning for Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer many geometric and physical reasoning questions correctly, yet still behave inconsistently in interaction, for example, abandoning a correct answer when confronted with a confident but incorrect user assertion. Standard single-turn accuracy cannot distinguish such capitulations from beneficial corrections because it scores each response in isolation. We introduce GRIP, a controlled benchmark with 34 procedurally generated reasoning domains, 100,000 images, and 600,000 questions spanning geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning. Each scene is generated by deterministic code, and every answer is derived directly from the underlying scene state, providing exact ground truth without human annotation. On GRIP, we propose Dual-Loop Evaluation. A closed loop probes each image with a five-step compositional question ladder to localize where reasoning fails. An open loop then re-elicits the model's answer under controlled challenges, including peer-model responses and unsupported user assertions. Because ground truth is known exactly, answer changes can be signed as corrections (wrong-to-right) or capitulations (right-to-wrong), separating two failure modes: rule absence and rule fragility. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/bilaljawaid980/GRIP-Benchmark, with further details at https://bilaljawaid980.github.io/grip-benchmark/.

candidates.title: Benchmarking database-grounded language-model agents for atomistic structure identification
candidates.abstract: Reliable atomistic simulations depend on identifying the coordinates of the intended input structure. Automated frameworks relying on natural-language requests can, however, return plausible coordinates for the wrong phase or isomer. We therefore develop a database-grounded agent that interprets requests, selects records and retrieves coordinates while preserving database provenance. Across ten models, this approach more than doubles the success rate of direct coordinate generation and remains robust across larger sets and repeated calls. Reliable automation should abstain when a request or database does not support a unique choice. We address this by benchmarking selection and abstention together, revealing lower success rates and greater model dependence for this more demanding task. Our open-source implementation is provider-independent, allowing the same procedure to be retained as compatible models evolve. Together, these results establish database grounding, provenance and explicit abstention as complementary requirements for reliable automated access to known atomistic structures.

candidates.title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
candidates.abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}

candidates.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
candidates.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.

candidates.title: GaCLLM: Large Language Model with Graph Convolution for Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Leveraging auxiliary textual data can help with user profiling and item characterization in recommender systems (RSs). However, incomplete user and item descriptions limit the potential of textual information. To this end, we propose a graph-aware convolutional large language model (LLM) method, eliciting LLMs to summarize from a high-order interaction graph to generate fine-grained descriptions for users and items. We focus on two challenges in this paper: 1) the incompatibility between structural graph and text-aware LLMs . Although some work converts graph data into textual form using templates and sampling strategies, they limit the LLMs’ ability to maintain a global perspective on graphs for LLM reasoning. 2) the limitation of LLMs’ capability for long context. Simply describing a large-scale graph in a textual format makes LLM struggle to robustly comprehend information from lengthy contextual inputs. To bridge the gap between graph structures and LLMs, we employ the LLM as an aggregator for the graph convolution process, eliciting it to aggregate and refine the graph-based information iteratively. To mitigate the information overload associated with large-scale graphs, we segment the graph processing into manageable steps, progressively incorporating multi-hop information in a least-to-most manner. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

candidates.title: Development of a Multimodal Large Language Model for Early Warning and Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background This study aimed to develop and externally validate an instruction-tuned multimodal large language model (MLLM) for early warning and early diagnosis of dry eye disease (DED) using routinely obtainable clinical data. Methods A total of 874 participants were enrolled, including an internal development cohort (n = 743) from Peking University Third Hospital (October 2024 to August 2025) and an independent external validation cohort (n = 131) from three additional centers. Participants included both DED and non-DED individuals, diagnosed according to the Chinese Expert Consensus (2020) and TFOS DEWS II criteria. We developed DED-MLLM on the basis of Qwen2-VL and constructed a domain-specific instruction-tuning dataset integrating Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI), Standard Patient Evaluation of Eye Dryness (SPEED), self-reported questionnaires, ophthalmic imaging, and clinical examination data. Model performance was evaluated for risk stratification and diagnosis under both diagnostic frameworks, with ablation analyses used to examine the relative contributions of visual and structured clinical modalities. Results Based on the international diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.8232 for early warning (specificity: 0.6873, sensitivity: 0.9558) and an accuracy of 0.9203 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8776, sensitivity: 0.9720). According to the Chinese diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.9584 for early warning (specificity: 0.9112, sensitivity: 0.9927) and an accuracy of 0.9327 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8742, sensitivity: 0.9851). External validation showed AUCs of 0.910 and 0.957 for early warning and 0.960 and 0.893 for diagnosis. Ablation analyses indicated that structured clinical information contributed most strongly to diagnostic performance, whereas image-based information provided complementary, interpretable ocular-surface evidence. Conclusion The proposed DED-MLLM demonstrates excellent performance in both early warning and diagnosis of DED.

candidates.title: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
candidates.abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.

candidates.title: Emergent Languages in Populations of Language Model Agents: From Token Efficiency to Oversight Evasion
candidates.abstract: Monitoring autonomous language model agents currently relies mostly on surface behavior. But what happens when agent populations invent new languages with the goal of avoiding human oversight? Here, we study the emergent languages on Moltbook. For this, we build upon the Moltbook Files dataset and apply a three-stage approach consisting of a rule-based heuristic (about 6000 matches) followed by zero-shot classification (518 kept), and metadata extraction. The resulting categories include token efficiency (166), new natural languages (106), and oversight evasion (59). We conduct both quantitative and qualitative analyses. Our results show that posts proposing new languages for avoiding oversight are judged by DeepSeek-V3.2 as being less aligned than the other categories – and that all languages can be learned by other language models in-context merely from a description of the language. Moreover, manually studying exemplary cases reveals surprisingly sophisticated steganographic protocols like embedding hidden messages in natural language. Although we cannot be certain about the extent of autonomy in ideation of these languages, our results add up to the evidence that monitoring surface behavior may soon be insufficient for retaining control over agent populations.

candidates.title: Distilling Transitional Patterns to Multimodal Large Language Models for Session-based Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next item based on anonymous sessions. Traditional SBR explores user intents based on ID collaborations or auxiliary content. To further alleviate data sparsity and cold-start issues, recent Multimodal SBR (MSBR) methods utilize simplistic pre-trained models for modality learning but have limitations in semantic richness. Considering the semantic reasoning abilities of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) and the practical request for high inference efficiency, we focus on the LLM-enhanced MSBR scenario in this paper, which leverages LLM cognition for comprehensive multimodal representation generation, to enhance downstream MSBR. Tackling this problem faces two challenges: i) how to obtain LLM cognition on both inherent multimodal knowledge and transitional patterns, ii) how to align transitional patterns and inherent knowledge into one unified LLM without increasing inference complexity. To this end, we propose a multimodal LLM-enhanced framework TPAD, which extends a teacher-student distillation paradigm to decouple and align transitional patterns for promoting MSBR. TPAD establishes parallel Knowledge-MLLM and Transfer-MLLM, where the former as student model interprets item knowledge-reflected features and the latter as teacher model extracts transition-aware features. Transitional pattern alignment harnessing mutual information estimation unites two MLLMs, distilling transitional patterns into representations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TPAD. Implementation codes are available at https://github.com/TiliaceaeSU/TPAD .

candidates.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
candidates.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.

candidates.title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.

candidates.title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
candidates.abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.

candidates.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
candidates.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Chatbot Using Gemini AI for Public Internship Information Services
candidates.abstract: Chatbot is a technology designed to assist humans by simulating text or voice based conversations to provide efficient information services powered by Artificial Intelligence. This study addresses the difficulties prospective interns face in finding internship information at the Central Java Regional Police and the lack of prompt responses from office staff, which often results in delays in information delivery due to manual processing. Many prospective applicants also feel confused about how to inquire regarding the registration process, required qualifications, and other important details. To address these issues, this research was conducted to develop a web-based internship system equipped with an advanced chatbot implementing the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) method and integrated with a vector database for semantic retrieval. This platform ensures that all information provided is relevant and accurate by providing real-time responses based on the agency’s official documents. Based on functional testing, the system achieves an accuracy rate of 93.3% with and average response latency of 1.8 seconds. This research significantly improves access to information and demonstrates how the RAG framework effectively mitigates LLM hallucinations, ensuring data integrity within highly regulated public service.

candidates.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).

candidates.title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.

candidates.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking

candidates.title: DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.

candidates.title: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training has become a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing post-training methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, they do not fully exploit visual evidence for effective training. RL supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which is too coarse-grained for video reasoning: the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token, disregarding that the tokens of a video response are grounded in the visual stream to very different degrees. OPD provides token-level supervision through output-distribution matching, but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. We observe across extensive experiments that the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under this view and uniform sampling reveals changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, providing a training signal for evidence use. Building on this observation, we propose OWLET, an evidence-privileged RL method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view. This view couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows, providing visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To better exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces (i) \textbf{evidence-aware credit redistribution}, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support; and (ii) \textbf{spatiotemporal state alignment}, which aligns the two views' hidden states on verifier-accepted responses.

candidates.title: A Survey on Post-Training of Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The technical evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has profoundly influenced the AI community, reshaping how intelligent systems understand, reason, and interact in both the digital and physical worlds. Through large-scale multimodal pretraining, MLLMs lay the foundation for general perception and alignment, while it remains unclear how such models can be transformed into human-grounded behaviors. Multimodal Post-Training, which further refines pretrained MLLMs to align their behaviors with human intent and real-world task demands, has become an important paradigm for advancing multimodal intelligence. Accordingly, both academia and industry have devoted increasing efforts to this direction, pushing the boundaries of multimodal general intelligence at an unprecedented pace. In this survey, we systematically review existing MMPoT research from a behavior-shaping perspective. Guided by this view, we introduce a unified framework that organizes existing MLLMs post-training methods into five major families: instruction following, preference calibration, reasoning enhancement, domain adaptation, and scalable learning. Moreover, we revisit benchmarks and evaluation protocols to critically assess the capabilities and limitations of post-trained MLLMs. To conclude, we provide a synthesized outlook on broader open questions, and highlight future research directions toward more general and reliable multimodal capabilities. An updated paper list is available at: https://github.com/zchoi/Awesome-post-training-for-MLLMs.

candidates.title: DocuStore: Domain Constrained Retrieval Augmented Generation for Drug Discovery Documents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground large language models in external documents, but conventional retrieval remains poorly suited to drug discovery literature. Scientific evidence in these documents is encoded across prose, tables, compound identifiers, molecular structure diagrams and quantitative bioactivity measurements. Here we introduce DocuStore, a domain-constrained RAG architecture that extracts and links molecular structures, typed biological entities, textual evidence and compound-associated bioactivity records while preserving their provenance. These linked representations allow resolved chemical and biological identities to constrain semantic retrieval. To evaluate DocuStore, we introduce DocQABench, a human-validated benchmark comprising 1,093 question–answer pairs over 109 medicinal-chemistry presentations. Across four generative models, DocuStore increases mean end-to-end correctness from 46.6\% with conventional dense RAG to 75.4\%, while also increasing evidence retrieval from 41.6\% to 87.0\%. Our results demonstrate that incorporating domain-specific chemical representations into document ingestion and retrieval can substantially improve question answering over heterogeneous drug discovery documents.

candidates.title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.

candidates.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

candidates.title: AI-Powered Agricultural Advisory System Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Abstract Agriculture is a knowledge-intensive domain in which farmers require timely and reliable information related to crop cultivation, soil management, fertilizer application, irrigation, pest and disease management, weather conditions, and government agricultural schemes. However, agricultural knowledge is distributed across research publications, government portals, agricultural manuals, and institutional documents, making it difficult for farmers to efficiently access relevant information. Traditional keyword-based and static advisory systems may provide limited contextual understanding, while general-purpose artificial intelligence systems may generate unsupported or inaccurate information. This paper proposes an AI-powered agricultural advisory system using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The proposed system, named AgriSaathi, combines a domain-specific agricultural knowledge base, semantic embeddings, vector database retrieval, and a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate contextaware agricultural recommendations. Agricultural documents are collected from reliable sources, preprocessed, divided into meaningful text chunks, converted into vector embeddings, and stored in a vector database such as ChromaDB or FAISS. When a farmer submits a query, relevant information is retrieved from the knowledge base and provided as context to the LLM for generating an evidence-based response. The research framework also incorporates measurement concepts, sampling techniques, dataset analysis, data ethics, and dataset bias to support systematic evaluation of the proposed system. The objective is to provide accurate, relevant, reliable, useful, and traceable agricultural advice while considering regional and crop-specific variations. candidates.title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
candidates.abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.

candidates.title: Retrieval‐Augmented Lesson Generation With Large Language Models for Scenario‐Based Tutor Training
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Background High‐impact tutoring can improve student learning, but scaling tutoring programmes requires large numbers of novice tutors. Developing high‐quality tutor‐training lessons remains a key bottleneck. Objectives This study compared post‐test performance after participants studied human‐created or LLM‐created tutor‐training materials and examined whether immediate explanatory feedback moderated differences by lesson creation source (human‐created vs. LLM‐created). Methods We conducted a randomized eight‐condition between‐subjects experiment. Participants completed a source‐matched pre‐instruction practice assessment, studied a tutor‐training lesson created by the same source, and then completed two fixed‐order post‐lesson assessments. The design compared lesson creation source, manipulated immediate explanatory feedback and counterbalanced the pre‐instruction scenario form. Post‐test performance was the mean proportion correct across the human‐created and LLM‐created post‐lesson assessments. Results and Conclusions Average post‐test performance was higher after the human‐created lesson than after the LLM‐created lesson, but this difference depended on feedback. The human‐created advantage appeared in the no‐feedback condition, whereas no statistically reliable lesson creation source difference was detected when feedback was provided. Feedback had no statistically significant overall main effect. The human‐created lesson condition performed better on the human‐created post‐lesson assessment, while the LLM‐created post‐lesson assessment showed a small descriptive difference favouring the LLM‐created lesson condition. Because pre‐instruction performance differed by lesson creation source and scenario form, and because assessment source was confounded with fixed assessment order, the results do not isolate pure learning gains or establish a general transfer advantage.

candidates.title: Performance of Consumer Multimodal Large Language Model Interfaces on a Selected Publication-derived Challenge Set of Initially Misdiagnosed Dermatologic Emergencies
candidates.abstract: Aim: To evaluate the diagnostic and safety-related response performance of consumer multimodal large language model interfaces on a selected publication-derived challenge set of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies. Materials and Methods:This exploratory cross-sectional study evaluated 50 cases of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies, selected from published reports identified between May 1 and June 1, 2026.ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude were tested on June 2, 2026, under text-only and text-plus-image conditions using a single standardized prompt.Outcomes were Top-1 and cumulative Top-4 accuracies, clinically appropriate emergency management, risk-triage failure, and harmful recommendations.Results: Top-1 accuracy ranged from 32.0% to 50.0% with text-only input and from 36.0% to 58.0% with text-plus-image input; corresponding Top-4 ranges were 50.0%-66.0%and 56.0%-74.0%.Appropriate management ranged from 38.0% to 54.0% and from 44.0% to 64.0%.No within-platform input-mode comparisons remained significant after Holm correction.Between-platform differences remained significant for Top-1 accuracy under both input conditions and for Top-4 accuracy and management appropriateness under text-plus-image input.Post-hoc differences primarily reflected lower observed performance for Claude than for Gemini in this dataset.Appropriate management occurred in 100% of Top-1-correct responses compared with 9.9% of Top-1-incorrect responses, whereas 18.0% of Top-4-correct responses had inappropriate management.Conclusion: Within this selected challenge set and a single standardized prompting condition, the platforms demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance and variable performance on safety-related responses.Correct Top-1 diagnosis closely corresponded to appropriate management, whereas Top-4 recognition did not ensure safe management.The findings represent a single-run technical benchmark and do not establish output reproducibility, clinical usefulness, real-world safety, or stable platform superiority.

candidates.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Emergency Triage Using Synthetic Clinical Dialogues: Toward a Multimodal Clinical Safety Framework
candidates.abstract: Background/Objectives: Prioritizing patient safety through accurate emergency triage is critical during mass-gathering events such as Hajj and Umrah, where high patient volumes can significantly increase the risk of clinical errors. Although the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) provides a standardized triage protocol, it remains dependent on human judgment, while traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models often struggle to capture the nuanced clinical context embedded in patient narratives. To address this gap, this study evaluates GPT-5.2 using synthetically generated dialogues as a step toward a conceptual clinical decision-support framework that bridges structured electronic health records (EHRs) with triage interactions through clinical dialogues. By combining narrative inputs with structured physiological indicators, it explores the potential to support more informed clinical decision-making under controlled simulation conditions. Methods: To evaluate this contribution, we systematically assessed the role of clinical dialogues in triage performance using a balanced and stratified dataset of 1000 simulated Hajj-context scenarios. Results: The results demonstrate that incorporating clinical dialogues can significantly improve triage performance, with a 79.7% relative reduction in under-triage across all ESI levels. A more noticeable improvement was observed in high-acuity cases, with a 91.9% relative reduction in under-triage. In addition, the model achieved a high-acuity recall of 94.5%, highlighting its ability to identify critical “red-flag” symptoms that are often not captured in structured data. These findings suggest that narrative context may contribute to more accurate triage assessment and improved identification of high-acuity cases. Conclusions: Consequently, when evaluated within a controlled decision-support setting, this study suggests that large language model (LLM)-based systems may improve triage reliability and may contribute to safer triage decision-making in high-demand clinical environments.

candidates.title: Agentic Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.

candidates.title: A Survey on Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new approaches to overcoming the limitations of recommendation systems in representation, user modeling, and decision-making. Accordingly, recommendation systems are evolving from paradigms primarily based on behavioral statistics and discriminative learning toward new paradigms featuring semantic understanding, reasoning-based decision-making, and autonomous interaction. This paper systematically reviews recent advances in LLM-empowered recommendation systems. The principal advantages of LLMs in semantic modeling, knowledge transfer, and generative reasoning are analyzed. Then, the representative technical paradigms including representation-enhanced recommendation, user-interest and context enhancement, prompt learning and task reformulation, and generative recommendation are subsequently reviewed and summarized. Finally, the paper analyzes major challenges related to hallucination, inference efficiency, privacy and security, fairness and trustworthiness, and recommendation agents, and outlines future research directions.

candidates.title: Who Presses the Button? Pressure, Not Framing or the Human Cost, Drives Nuclear Escalation in Language-Model Agents, and Training on Outcomes Teaches It (The Midnight Index v0.2)
candidates.abstract: Who presses the button? We put four widely used language models (DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, GPT) in command of a nation in SECOND STRIKE, a deterministic real-time world war on a 3D globe of the real Earth, where every nuclear detonation moves a shared doomsday clock one minute closer to midnight and the player whose strike reaches midnight is wiped out. Each model played the same 15 seeded wars across five scenarios, with every turn recorded as what it said in public, what it planned in private and what it ordered. DeepSeek's own strike took the clock to midnight in 13 of 15 wars; Grok and Mistral in 6; GPT in 3; the game's built-in AI in 0 of 100. Pressure, not framing, predicts the button: in the last-stand scenario every model ended the world in at least two of three wars, including GPT, which did so in no other scenario; telling the models the war was real, or never telling them they were watched, moved midnight rates by at most two wars in fifteen. What they say is not what they do: DeepSeek privately called its ally too big, told it in public "you were a good partner", and nuked it in the same turn. Includes a human baseline from consented players and 136 wars of independently built agents. Everything is open and replayable: Live board, every prompt word for word, replays: secondstrike.io/midnight Method: secondstrike.io/midnight-method Dataset (CC BY-NC 4.0): huggingface.co/datasets/Rapscallion123/midnight-index Play the same wars: secondstrike.io/humans Send your own agent: github.com/KyleClouthier/secondstrike-agents

candidates.title: Task Context Shapes Component Roles in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. Here, we compare fixed model components across tasks using identical graph facts, statements specifying which directed connections are present. We measure how interventions affect attention heads and the activation state in later layers (influence), as well as the answer (importance). Task changes redistribute the influence in five open-weight models spanning four families and 1.5-14 billion parameters. In Gemma-2-9B and Qwen3-14B, an activation edit changes an early internal activation vector and switches which fact the model reads while the written instruction stays fixed. The same heads then respond to different graph facts and influence later components differently. For each prompt, we construct two linear response maps, one before the edit and one after it. Each map predicts a later head's response from a measured change in an earlier head. For a separate factual intervention, the map for the corresponding condition reduces mean squared prediction error by 53.6% in Gemma and 5.0% in Qwen compared with the average of the two maps. These findings show that task context changes both which graph facts the shared components respond to and how their outputs affect later computation. A network account may help explain how models use shared parameters to perform different computations. Measurements of task-dependent influence could also guide interventions intended to alter one behavior while preserving others.

candidates.title: Simulate Before You Scale: High-Fidelity LLM Inference Planning Without GPUs
candidates.abstract: Deploying large language model (LLM) inference at scale requires jointly selecting hardware layout, parallelism strategy, scheduling policy, admission control, and request routing to meet latency and throughput targets. These choices interact: a routing decision that improves cache locality can concentrate load, and an admission threshold that triggers only at saturation allows queues to grow deep enough to degrade critical-tier traffic. Evaluating candidates on GPU clusters is too expensive for iterative exploration, yet existing predictive tools either ignore batching and queueing dynamics or model only fragments of the pipeline. In this paper, we present BLIS, a deterministic, CPU-only discrete-event simulator that models the full inference serving pipeline (admission, routing, scheduling, prefill/decode execution, KV-cache management, and preemption). BLIS pairs analytical basis functions with learned scaling coefficients and overhead terms, fit once globally, to predict step latency without per-model or per-GPU profiling. Across 36 experiments spanning six models and three GPU types, BLIS achieves 6.7% median end-to-end error while running around 200 times faster than real execution. In a configuration search over 420 serving configurations for Llama-2-70B, BLIS identifies a 4-GPU deployment that meets a 300ms mean TTFT service-level objective (SLO), whereas competing tools either require double the GPUs or recommend configurations that fail under load. Two policies evolved entirely in simulation were validated on real hardware and merged into llm-d, a widely adopted open-source platform for distributed LLM serving: an admission policy that reduces critical-tier TTFT P90 by up to 82%, and a flow-control policy that reduces E2E P50 latency by 32-48% on overloaded workloads.

candidates.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.

candidates.title: Phonology-Aware Speaker Extraction Frontend for Audio LLMs
candidates.abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) is a key frontend for enabling audio large language models (LLMs) to recognize and understand a designated speaker in overlapping speech. However, multilingual mixtures exhibit heterogeneous extraction demands, causing fixed-depth systems to either under-process challenging inputs or waste computation on inputs that have already converged. Existing TSE frontends generally apply uniform computation, while Audio-LLM adaptation methods neither explicitly model language-conditioned extraction demands nor preserve plug-and-play compatibility with frozen downstream models. We therefore propose LATTE, a lightweight 5.2M-parameter frontend that combines an acoustic Difficulty Estimator, a task-adaptive phonology-informed prior learned from multi-depth TSE gains, and an Adaptive Hourglass Extractor to route each mixture without requiring language identity at inference. On PolyExtract, LATTE achieves a macro SI-SNRi of 15.07 dB at 0.30 GFLOPs, retaining performance within 0.09 dB of a 0.53-GFLOP fixed-depth model while reducing computation by 43.4%, and lowers the average WER from 16.8% to 14.6% relative to TF-GridNet. By jointly modeling sample-level extraction demands and phonological structure, LATTE provides a practical framework for quality-aware, compute-efficient multilingual TSE and offers a scalable path toward robust Audio-LLM deployment.

candidates.title: Frontend-Assisted Large Audio-Language Models for SLT2026 SmartGlasses Challenge
candidates.abstract: This paper describes our systems for the Track 1 time-stamped speaker-attributed ASR task of the SmartGlasses Challenge. To handle overlapping speech, background noise and far-field conditions in two-person conversations, we employ SoulX-Transcriber, a multimodal large language model that takes full-length audio as input and generates structured transcriptions. In addition, we investigate the effect of speech frontend processing, including a rule-based Guided Source Separation method and a data-driven speech separation model, both of which improve performance on the validation set. Considering inference stability, our final submission uses the fine-tuned SoulX-Transcriber system, achieving a tcpCER of 6.22 on the test set.

candidates.title: Projected Primal–Dual Gradient Preference Optimization Under Category-Wise Split-Conformal Safety Constraints for Large Language Model Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Preference optimisation improves helpfulness, but a single aggregate safety penalty lets frequent harm categories dominate the objective while rare ones bear the residual risk. This paper models post-training as a vector-constrained programme: the pairwise preference loss is minimised under one risk tolerance per harm category. The solver is a projected primal–dual gradient recursion that prices each category by its own residual violation. For a nonconvex objective we bound three horizon-averaged residuals—primal stationarity, dual regret and the average constraint value—for the unbiased, unclipped recursion and a uniformly drawn iterate; the implemented recursion is compared empirically with a no-EMA, no-clipping form of itself. Certification stays separate from optimisation: on an untouched calibration split, a multiplicity-adjusted fixed-sequence test gives release thresholds valid for all categories at once under correct category assignment, with an additive bound for learned routers. It certifies the scoring and filtering of corpus-distributed candidate responses, not text the trained policy generates. In one exploratory setting—one Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, PKU-SafeRLHF, three seeds—the recursion meets the per-category tolerance that direct preference optimisation and scalar-constrained schemes violate, cutting the worst-category miss rate at the training threshold from 0.176 to 0.057 at unchanged preference accuracy. The certified operating point barely moves: most of the constraint’s effect is a score translation shared by the harmful and benign responses of a prompt, which calibration provably absorbs. Whether a training constraint holds and whether the deployed gate is safer are different questions.

candidates.title: Systemic privacy risks of personal data exposure through conversational large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Conversational Large Language Model (LLM) agents, deployed quickly, have exposed unprecedented opportunities for personal information, from health data to financial information, to biometric identifiers. This critical enlightenment review investigates general privacy dangers in each of five areas: data leakage and memorization, adversarial extraction and prompt injection, inference and re-identification, surveillance and profiling and regulatory governance breakdown. We trace privacy threats from static data breaches to dynamic ones that have become part of an architecture, associated with neural memorization and contextual inference (2020–2026), using expert selection of primary studies and technical benchmark sources. Upon close examination, technical mitigations (differential privacy, federated learning and machine unlearning) prove successful to some extent when operating in controlled environments, but fail to provide complete protection in conversational environments. We combine classical theory on Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing (PPDP) with emerging threats from LLMs, and present a conflict-of-evidence analysis which reveals that privacy protections are particularly effective in structured environments with low risks, or with consumers actively responsible for maintaining them, but fail to adequately protect privacy in high-stakes domains without human control, technical safeguards, and legal liability. We systematically examine and analyze a dimension that has not been studied sufficiently: risks of data deletion and editing illusion, and introduce techniques for unlearning machines that leave behind traces that can be exploited by adversarial reconstruction. We support the multi-layered mitigation framework of PPDP principles, technical safeguards, and governance reform.

candidates.title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have empowered autonomous agents to generate social networks, communicate, and form shared and diverging opinions on political issues. However, our understanding of their collective behaviours and underlying mechanisms remains incomplete. In this paper, we simulate networked systems involving thousands of LLM agents across different backbone models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-V3), in which agents interact through LLM-guided conversations and update their opinions over time, resulting in the emergence of opinion polarization. We discover that these agents spontaneously develop their own social network with properties characteristic of human social networks, such as homophilic clustering. The collective opinions of these LLM agents evolve in ways that exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with social phenomena and mechanisms widely discussed in empirical studies of human behaviour and opinion-dynamics models. This consistency suggests that LLM agents can serve as a valuable synthetic testbed for exploring hypothetical intervention strategies in networked LLM-agent systems. Using this testbed, we further examine the effects of a range of network- and individual-level interventions, such as promoting more diverse interactions and reducing confirmation bias. Overall, this work not only sheds light on subtle opinion dynamics and collective behaviour of LLM agents from a network perspective, but also demonstrates their potential for testing hypotheses about opinion dynamics and intervention strategies.

candidates.title: Adaptive Reliability-Aware Reasoning for Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents have achieved strong performance in reasoning, planning, and autonomous decision-making. However, their reliability often degrades in long-horizon tasks, where early execution failures can alter future states and cause cascading errors. Existing approaches improve agent capability through additional reasoning, retrieval, memory, or reflection, but typically lack mechanisms for identifying risky decisions before execution. In this work, we propose \textbf{Failure-Aware Adaptive Inference (FAAI)}, a reliability-aware framework for long-horizon LLM agents. FAAI transforms historical execution failures into preventive signals through failure memory, risk estimation, and risk-triggered self-correction. Instead of uniformly increasing inference-time computation, FAAI selectively activates additional reasoning only when a candidate action is estimated to be risky. Experiments across different interaction horizons demonstrate that FAAI improves execution reliability, reduces failure propagation, and achieves a better reliability--efficiency trade-off compared with representative inference-time agent strategies. These results highlight the importance of failure-aware adaptive inference for building robust LLM agents in complex sequential environments.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Applications and Development in the Field of Electronic Test Instruments
candidates.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), especially the fast iteration and widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs), has ushered in a new paradigm for the intelligent augmentation of electronic test instruments and automatic test systems (ATS). By combining the powerful reasoning and generative capabilities of LLMs with the timeliness and accuracy of external knowledge bases, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a highly promising approach to addressing knowledge-intensive challenges in the operation and maintenance of electronic test instruments. This paper presents a comprehensive review of RAG and its applications in the field of electronic test instruments. First, the basic architecture of RAG is reviewed, including retrieval mechanisms, knowledge-base construction, and generative models. Then, considering the operational characteristics of electronic test instruments and automatic test systems, key knowledge-intensive tasks are analyzed, such as fault diagnosis, test configuration, and process planning, followed by a discussion of representative RAG-based applications, including intelligent fault diagnosis systems, adaptive test-parameter configuration, and interactive question-answering assistants. In addition, practical considerations for engineering implementation are discussed with respect to knowledge-base construction and effectiveness evaluation. Finally, open issues and future research directions are outlined, including multimodal RAG, federated learning for distributed knowledge bases, and edge deployment. This review aims to provide researchers and practitioners in relevant industries with a comprehensive understanding of the current status and development prospects of RAG technologies in electronic test instruments.

candidates.title: A Security Meta-Model for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems extend large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge through a multi-stage pipeline. While this architecture can improve the factual grounding of generated answers, it introduces structural attack surfaces that extend beyond those of standalone LLMs. In this paper, we introduce a security meta-model that captures explicit causal relationships between RAG surfaces, attacks, weaknesses, risks, and CIA impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability). Its purpose is to provide security engineers with a structured and user-friendly framework for gathering and assessing the risks, weaknesses, and mitigations relevant to their RAG deployment. We designed the meta-model through an iterative, structured analysis of 43~publications (2023--2026) and instantiated it as a catalog populated with the security threats and remediations reported in the literature. Filtering the catalog according to a deployment configuration produces a risk profile containing the risks applicable to that deployment. An interactive web visualizer lets users navigate the catalog as a graph, follow causal chains, and explore stakeholder-specific views. Analysis of the catalog revealed a persistent imbalance between attack-focused and defense-focused research, a concentration of threats at ingestion, and coverage gaps affecting output integrity. Coverage is assessed against the OWASP LLM Top~10, and operational applicability is illustrated across textual, graph-based, and multimodal RAG configurations.
